ggg


The best local alignment is GGG against GGG, with a score of 6. The global alignments had to include the A in GAGGG and the CT in GGGCT, which cost 5 points.

title: 53  Pairwise alignment
text:
Better gap scores
So far every gap position has cost the same, wherever it is and however long the gap. Real alignment programs score gaps more carefully, in two ways.

Gaps at the ends
Suppose you align a gene sequence you have just read from a sample with a reference sequence that starts a little earlier and ends a little later. The gaps at the ends of the alignment do not reflect any insertion or deletion. They are there only because one sequence was read over a shorter stretch. Penalizing them as if they were real mutations makes the alignment worse. Many programs therefore score gaps at the ends of a global alignment differently, often not at all.
In the table, end gaps live along the edges. The first row and the first column hold alignments that begin with a series of gaps. The last row and the last column are where alignments that end with a series of gaps pass through: once the traceback is in the last column, every step up adds a base from the left sequence against a gap at the end of the alignment.








Figure 53.16: Gaps at the beginning of an alignment are steps along the first row or column (blue). Gaps at the end are steps along the last row or column (orange).






Exercise 53-6
SOLO
You want to change Needleman-Wunsch so that gaps at the ends of the alignment score 0 instead of the usual gap score. Using Figure 53.16, find the two places in the algorithm that must change. Then decide what the alignment of GGGCT and GAGGG would look like if end gaps were free. You do not need to fill in a new table for this; think about which bases would have to be left hanging at the ends.






TipShow the answer





The first place is the first row and column, which get 0 instead of multiples of the gap score. The second place is the last row and column: a step to the left within the last row, or a step up within the last column, adds a gap at the end of the alignment, so it should use the end-gap score of 0 instead of the gap score.
With free end gaps, GGGCT and GAGGG can overlap like this, with three pairs of matching Gs and only the overhanging bases against gaps:









That scores \(3 \times 2 = 6\), against the best score of 1 when end gaps cost −2 each.






Long gaps
A single mutation can insert or delete many bases at once. A gap of 11 bases is therefore much more likely to be one event than eleven separate events next to each other, and it should not cost eleven times as much as a gap of one base. With the gap score we have used so far, a gap of length \(\ell\) costs
\[
\gamma(\ell) = -d \, \ell,
\]
where \(d\) is the cost per gap position. This is called a linear gap score. The alternative is an affine gap score, which charges more for opening a gap than for extending one:
\[
\gamma(\ell) = -d - (\ell - 1) \, e,
\]
where \(d\) is the cost of opening the gap and \(e\) the cost of each additional position, with \(e\) much smaller than \(d\). An affine gap score prefers one long gap to several short ones, as mutation does.

Exercise 53-7
SOLO
With a linear gap score and \(d = 10\), what does a gap of length 11 cost? With an affine gap score, \(d = 10\) and \(e = 1\), what does the same gap cost? And what do two separate gaps of length 1 cost with the affine score?






TipShow the answer





Linear: \(-10 \times 11 = -110\). Affine: \(-10 - 10 \times 1 = -20\). Two separate gaps of length 1 cost \(-10\) each, so \(-20\) in total: the same as the single gap of length 11.



An affine gap score seems to break the algorithm. To score a step up into a cell, we now need to know whether the best alignment ending in the cell above already ended in a gap (and we extend it) or not (and we open a new one). The fix is to keep three scores in every cell instead of one: the best score of an alignment that ends with a pair of bases, the best that ends with a base from the left sequence against a gap, and the best that ends with a gap against a base from the top sequence. Each of the three is computed from the three scores in one neighbor. A diagonal step adds the score of the base pair to the best of the three. A step down from the cell above extends the gap if that alignment already ended in the same kind of gap, and opens a new gap otherwise. The step from the left works the same way.
Figure 53.17 shows this for a single cell. The upper left number in each cell is the pair score, the upper right is the gap-in-the-top-sequence score, which only a step down can extend, and the lower left is the gap-in-the-left-sequence score, which only a step to the right can extend. With a linear gap score (left), keeping three numbers changes nothing: the largest of the new cell’s three scores is the 4 we would have computed anyway. With an affine score (right), the numbers differ, and keeping all three is what lets the algorithm tell opening from extending (Gotoh, 1982).








Figure 53.17: Keeping three scores per cell. In each cell, upper left: best alignment ending in a pair of bases; upper right: ending in a base from the left sequence against a gap; lower left: ending in a gap against a base from the top sequence. Each new score is the largest of the three sums in one neighbor. Left: linear gap score of −1. Right: affine gap score with opening −5 and extension −1.





Three scores per cell means three times the work per cell, but the number of cells is the same. Filling in the table for two sequences of length \(n\) takes about \(n^2\) steps either way, which is written \(O(n^2)\). Doubling the length of both sequences makes the work four times as large. That is a lot for two whole genomes, but tiny compared with trying all \(2 \times 10^{75}\) alignments of two sequences of 100 bases.

title: 53  Pairwise alignment
text:
Alignment tools
You will rarely fill in an alignment table by hand again after this chapter, and after the project you will rarely need to write the code either. The European Bioinformatics Institute offers EMBOSS Needle for global alignment and EMBOSS Water for local alignment, both on the web. For DNA, they use EDNAFULL with an affine gap score that costs 10 to open and 0.5 to extend. Needle does not penalize end gaps unless you ask it to. The PairwiseAligner in Biopython does the same jobs from Python: its mode attribute chooses global or local alignment, and open_gap_score and extend_gap_score set an affine gap score.

Then compare the results with the alignments printed in that section. title: 54  Project: Pairwise alignment
text:
Make an “empty” matrix
We start by making a list of lists (a matrix) with the right shape but only holds None values. We use the None values as placeholders, which you can later replace with scores. You can think of it as an empty matrix into which you can fill scores, just as we did in the lectures. If you want to align two sequences like AT and GAT, you want a matrix with three rows and four columns. Note that the matrix must have one more row than the number of bases in sequence one and one more column than the number of bases in sequence two.
Write a function, empty_matrix, that takes two arguments

An integer (which represents the length of sequence one + 1).
An integer (which represents the length of sequence two + 1).

The function must return:

A list of lists. The number of sub-lists must be equal to the first integer argument. Each sublist must contain a number of None values equal to the second integer argument.

Example usage:
empty_matrix(3, 4)
returns a list with three lists each of length four:
[[None, None, None, None], [None, None, None, None], [None, None, None, None]]
Even though this is a list of lists, we can think of it as a three-by-four matrix:
[[None, None, None, None], 
 [None, None, None, None], 
 [None, None, None, None]]
You can use print_matrix to print the matrix with the sequence bases along the left and top margins. Printing an “empty” matrix will looks like this:
          G    A    T
  None None None None
A None None None None
T None None None None


Prepare the dynamic programming matrix
Now that you can make a matrix with the correct dimensions, you need to write a function that fills in the top row and the left column with multiples of the gap score. E.g., if the gap score is -2, you want the matrix to look something like this when you print it with print_dp_matrix:
          G    A    T
     0   -2   -4   -6
A   -2 None None None
T   -4 None None None
Write a function, prepare_dp_matrix, which takes three arguments:

An integer (which represents the length of sequence one plus one)
An integer (which represents the length of sequence two plus one)
An integer, which represents the gap_score used for alignment.

The function must return:

A list of lists. The number of sub-lists must be equal to the first integer argument. The values in the first sub-list must be multiples of the gap score given as the third argument. The first elements of the remaining sub-lists must be multiples of the gap score. All remaining elements of sub-lists must be None.

Example usage:
prepare_dp_matrix(3, 4, -2)
must return:
[[0, -2, -4, -6], [-2, None, None, None], [-4, None, None, None]]






NoteHint 1





You can call empty_matrix inside prepare_dp_matrix to get an empty matrix to fill in. Remember that the matrix needs to have as many rows as we can align bases from sequence one. Since that includes zero aligned bases the number of rows must be equal the length of sequence one plus one. Same logic goes for the sequence two and the columns.
dp_matrix = empty_matrix(len(seq1)+1, len(seq2)+1)









NoteHint 2





When you have a matrix filled with None values, all you need to do is replace the right None values with multiples of the gap score. For example, the third element in the first sub-list is dp_matrix[2][0], for which you would need to assign the value 2 times the gap score. In the same way dp_matrix[3][0] should be 3 times the gap score. So, you need to figure out which elements you should replace and which pairs of indexes you need to access those elements. Then, use range to generate those indexes and for-loops to loop them over.





Prepare the traceback matrix
When we fill in the dynamic programming matrix, each score is computed from one of the three cells surrounding it left to top. To be able to do the traceback at the end we must record which one we used. I.e. if the traceback needs to go “up”, “left”, or to the “diagonal” cell. The traceback matrix has the same shape as the dynamic programming matrix and should end up with each cell filled with U for “up”, L for “left”, or “D” for diagonal. You need to prepare this matrix by filling the same rows as you did preparing the dynamic programming matrix (except for the top left one) like this:
          A    T
  None    L    L
G    U None None
A    U None None
T    U None None
Write a function, prepare_traceback_matrix, which takes two arguments:

An integer (which represents the length of sequence one plus one)
An integer (which represents the length of sequence two plus one)

The function must return:

A list of lists. The number of sub-lists must be equal to the first integer argument. In the first sub-list, all but the first value must all be 'L'. The first values of the remaining sub-lists must all be 'U'. All remaining elements of sub-lists must be None.

Example usage:
prepare_traceback_matrix(3, 4)
must return:
[[0, 'L', 'L', 'L'], ['U', None, None, None], ['U', None, None, None]]






NoteHint 1





You can call empty_matrix inside prepare_traceback_matrix to get an empty matrix to fill in. Remember that the matrix needs to have as many rows as we can align bases from sequence one. Since that includes zero aligned bases the number of rows must be equal the length of sequence one plus one. Same logic goes for the sequence two and the columns.
dp_matrix = empty_matrix(len(seq1)+1, len(seq2)+1)

title: 54  Project: Pairwise alignment
text:
Fill the matrices
Now that we can fill the top row and left column of our matrices, we can start thinking about how to fill them in completely.
For that, we need a score matrix of match scores. In Python, that is most easily represented as a dictionary of dictionaries like this:

score_matrix = {'A': {'A': 2, 'T': 0, 'G': 0, 'C': 0},
                'T': {'A': 0, 'T': 2, 'G': 0, 'C': 0},
                'G': {'A': 0, 'T': 0, 'G': 2, 'C': 0},
                'C': {'A': 0, 'T': 0, 'G': 0, 'C': 2}}

That lets you get the score for matching an A with a T like this: score_matrix['A']['T']. Note that the match scores are only for uppercase letters (A, T, G, C).
Write a function, fill_matrices, which takes four arguments:

A string, which represents the first sequence.
A string, which represents the second sequence.
A dictionary of dictionaries like the one shown above, which represents match scores.
An integer, which represents the gap score.

The function must return:

A tuple of two values, The first must be a list of lists of numeric values representing the the filled in dynamic programming matrix. The second must be a list of lists representing the the filled in traceback matrix.

Example usage: If score_matrix is defined as above, then

fill_matrices("GTC", "GC", score_matrix, -2)

must return:
([[0, -2, -4], [-2, 0, -2], [-4, 0, 0], [-6, -2, 2]],
 [[None, 'L', 'L'], ['U', 'D', 'D'], ['U', 'D', 'D'], ['U', 'U', 'D']])
When printed with print_matrix, the first shoould look like this:
      G  A  T
   0 -2 -4 -6
A -2  0  0 -2
T -4 -2  0  2
and the second should look like this:
          A    T
  None    L    L
G    U    D    D
A    U    D    D
T    U    U    D






NoteHint 1





You can call prepare_dp_matrix and prepare_traceback_matrix inside fill_matrices to get the matrices with the top rows and left columns filled in. Assuming seq1 is sequence one and seq2 is sequence two, then you can do it like this:
dp_matrix = prepare_dp_matrix(len(seq1)+1, len(seq2)+1, gap_score)
traceback_matrix = prepare_traceback_matrix(len(seq1)+1, len(seq2)+1)









NoteHint 2





To fill in the rest of the cells in each matrix, you need two nested for-loops to produce the indexes of the i,j elements in the cells to fill in:
for i in range(1, len(seq1)+1):
    for j in range(1, len(seq2)+1):
        ...
Each combination of i and j lets you access an element dp_matrix[i][j] in dp_matrix or assign a value to it.









NoteHint 3





The value to assign to each dp_matrix[i][j] is the maximum of three values:

The value of the cell to the left plus the gap score: left = dp_matrix[i][j-1] + gap_score.
The value of the cell above plus the gap score: up = dp_matrix[i-1][j] + gap_score.
The value of the diagonal cell plus the score aligning the base with index i-1 in sequence one (base1 = seq1[i-1]) with the base with index j-1 in sequence two (base2 = seq2[j-1]): diag = dp_matrix[i-1][j-1] + score_matrix[base1][base2].

I.e., max_score = max(left, up, diag)









NoteHint 4





If you have defined left, up, diag, and max_score inside the for loop as in Hint 3, and assigned max_score to dp_matrix[i][j] all that remains is to also fill in the corresponding cell, tb_matrix[i][j], in the traceback matrix. It should be 'D' if max_score == diag, 'U' if max_score == up, and 'L' otherwise.

title: 54  Project: Pairwise alignment
text:
Traceback
Write a function, traceback, which takes four arguments:

A string, which represents the first sequence.
A string, which represents the second sequence.
A list of lists, which represents a traceback matrix.

The function must return:

A tuple of two strings that together represent the alignment of the sequences given as arguments one and two as specified by the traceback matrix.

Example usage: If traceback is defined as above, then

traceback_matrix = [
    [None, 'L', 'L', 'L'],
    ['U', 'D', 'D', 'L'],
    ['U', 'D', 'D', 'D'],
    ['U', 'U', 'D', 'L']
    ]
traceback('ATA', 'TAG', traceback_matrix)

must return:
('ATA-', '-TAG')
This is difficult one. Give it shot, but displair. You can see an explained solution in the reveal below:






NoteThe traceback function






def traceback(seq1, seq2, tb_matrix):
    aln1, aln2 = '', ''                        # Strings we will extend backwards.
    row, col = len(seq1), len(seq2)            # Start with last row and col.
    while row > 0 and col > 0:                 # While not at upper or left matrix edge.
        c1, c2 = '-', '-'                      # We let the two chars default to gaps.
        if tb_matrix[row][col] in ['U', 'D']:  # Came from row above.
            c1 = seq1[row-1]                   # A base from seq1 is aligned.
            row = row - 1                      # Next cell is in row above..
        if tb_matrix[row][col] in ['L', 'D']:  # Came from col to the left.
            c2 = seq2[col-1]                   # A base from seq2 is aligned.
            col = col - 1                      # Next cell is in col to the left.
        aln1 = c1 + aln1                       # Add symbol to from of aln1.
        aln2 = c2 + aln2                       # Add symbol to from of aln1.
    while row > 0:                             # At left edge of matrix.
        aln1 = seq1[row-1] + aln1              # A base from seq1 is aligned.
        aln2 = '-' + aln2                      # No base from seq2 is aligned.
        row = row - 1                          # Move up along the left matrix edge.
    while col > 0:                             # At upper edge of matrix.
        aln1 = '-' + aln1                      # No base from seq2 is aligned.
        aln2 = seq2[col-1] + aln2              # A base from seq2 is aligned.
        col = col - 1                          # Move left along the upper matrix edge.
    return aln1, aln2

title: 55  BLAST
text:
The original BLAST
If you have a sequence, BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) finds similar sequences in a large database in seconds rather than days. This chapter explains how. BLAST builds on ideas you already know from Chapter 53, adds a shortcut that trades some guarantee for speed, and includes a statistical measure of how much to trust what it finds.
In Chapter 53 you met local alignment and the Smith-Waterman algorithm (Smith and Waterman, 1981), which is guaranteed to find the best local alignment of two sequences. So why not align your sequence to every sequence in the database and keep the best ones?
The answer is arithmetic. Smith-Waterman fills in a table with one cell for every pair of positions, one from each sequence. Aligning a 1,000-base gene to another 1,000-base gene means filling in a million cells, which is nothing for a computer. But a database is not one sequence. The human genome alone is about 3.1 billion bases long, so aligning a single gene against it means filling in \(1000 \times 3.1 \times 10^9 = 3.1 \times 10^{12}\) cells. A computer that fills in a hundred million cells per second needs 31,000 seconds, more than eight and a half hours, and NCBI’s databases hold the genomes of a great many species besides. Now picture an NCBI server answering thousands of searches every hour.
Something has to give, and what BLAST gives up is the guarantee. BLAST is a heuristic: a shortcut that usually finds the best alignments, but is not promised to. In exchange, it is very fast. The shortcut rests on one biological observation. If two sequences are related, the alignment between them almost always contains a few short stretches where the two sequences are identical or nearly so. So rather than aligning everything to everything, BLAST first looks for those short stretches, and only spends time aligning where it finds one. The earlier FASTA program (Lipman and Pearson, 1985) had already used this idea. BLAST, the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (Altschul et al., 1990), made it faster and gave it a solid statistical footing. The paper describing it is one of the most cited scientific papers ever written.
The original BLAST works in four steps:
The figures and numbers in this chapter come from a small Python version of each step, running behind the page. It is slow and simple where the real BLAST is fast and clever, but it does the same thing. We start with DNA, where everything is simplest, and turn to proteins in the section on protein search.

title: 55  BLAST
text:
Chop your sequence, the query, into short overlapping words, and list every word that scores well against one of them.
Scan the database for those words. Each occurrence is a hit.
Extend each hit in both directions into a longer alignment, and stop when the score starts falling.
Decide whether the alignments found are better than what you would expect by chance.



Step 1: overlapping words
To chop a query into words of length \(w\), slide a window of width \(w\) along it, one base at a time. A query of length \(L\) has \(L - w + 1\) such words, because the last word must start \(w - 1\) bases before the end, or it would be too short. Our example query, TGCATGCCAGTTACGGATCAAG, has 22 bases and so 19 words of length 4. A gene of 1,000 bases has 990 words of length 11. Figure 55.1 shows the words of the first twelve bases for two word sizes. Each base belongs to up to \(w\) words, and every word overlaps the next one in all but one base.








Figure 55.1: The overlapping words of the first twelve bases of the query, for word size 3 (left) and word size 6 (right). Longer words are fewer, and each one is a longer and rarer string.





One option is to look only for exact copies of the query’s words. But a word in a related sequence may differ from the query word by a base or two, and BLAST lets you decide how different it can be. To do that, it scores two words against each other position by position, using a score matrix like the one in the pairwise alignment chapter. The standard DNA scores in blastn are 2 for a match and −3 for a mismatch. A word of length \(w\) with \(k\) mismatches therefore scores \(2(w - k) - 3k = 2w - 5k\) against the query word: ACGT scores 8 against itself, 3 against AGGT, and −12 against TCGA.
The neighborhood of a word is every word that scores at least some threshold \(T\) against it. At \(T = 3\), the neighborhood of ACGT holds ACGT itself and the twelve words that differ from it in exactly one base: three other bases at each of four positions. The left side of Figure 55.2 shows them, with the changed base in orange. The right side shows how neighborhood size depends on both settings. Lowering \(T\) lets in words with more mismatches, and the neighborhood grows in steps, one step for each extra mismatch allowed. For the same \(T\), a longer word has a bigger neighborhood, because there are more places for a mismatch to go.








Figure 55.2: Left: the neighborhood of ACGT at threshold T = 3, with each changed base shown in orange. Right: the number of words in the neighborhood of a DNA word as the threshold T changes, for word sizes 3 to 6 (note the logarithmic axis).





Here is the trade-off that runs through the rest of this chapter. A big neighborhood (small \(w\), low \(T\)) means a related sequence is likely to contain at least one of the words, even if it has drifted far from the query. But it also means more chance hits in unrelated sequences, and each one takes time to check. A small neighborhood is fast but misses distant relatives. We measure this trade-off in the section on word size and threshold.
BLAST puts all the neighborhoods into one lookup table: for every word, it records the query positions it is a neighbor of. In Python, that is a dictionary from words to lists of positions. With \(T = 8\), the top score for a word of length 4, each neighborhood holds only the word itself, so the table records only where each of the query’s own words appears: 19 words, each at its own position. With \(T = 3\), each word brings its twelve one-mismatch neighbors along, and the table grows to 180 words. BLAST builds the table once, from the query alone, before it looks at the database.


Step 2: scanning the database
Now BLAST walks along each database sequence, the subject, one word at a time and looks each word up in the table. Looking up a key in a dictionary is very fast and takes about the same time no matter how big the dictionary is, which is why BLAST can afford to do it for every position in a database of billions of bases. Every time BLAST finds a word, it records a hit as a pair of positions \((i, j)\): where the word is in the query and where it is in the subject.
Our query, scanned against the subject CCGTATTGCATGCAAGTTACGCATCAAGTTCGA with exact words of length 4, gives 15 hits. For 11 of them, the difference \(j - i\) is the same, 6. That difference is called the diagonal of a hit. If you draw the query down one side of a grid and the subject along the other, as in the alignment tables of Chapter 53, all hits with the same \(j - i\) lie on the same diagonal line through the grid, and they belong to the same ungapped alignment. Here, they mark where the subject contains a copy of the query starting 6 bases in. The few hits on other diagonals are chance matches of short words. Such a grid of hits is called a dot plot, and Figure 55.3 shows it for our query and subject. The gaps in the diagonal line are where the copy differs from the query.








Figure 55.3: A dot plot of the hits of the query in the subject, for word size 4 and exact matches. Each dot is a hit. The hits on one diagonal line mark the copy of the query in the subject.





Keep the diagonals in mind. They are the key to the improved BLAST of 1997.


Step 3: extending a hit
A hit is only a few bases. To see whether it is part of something bigger, BLAST extends it, one base at a time, first to the right and then to the left, adding the score of each new pair of bases. The extension has no gaps: it just walks along the diagonal.
When should it stop? The score goes up when the bases agree, and down when they don’t, so a single mismatch shouldn’t end the extension. BLAST remembers the best score it has seen so far and stops when the score has dropped more than some amount \(X\) below that best. Then it trims the alignment back to where it saw the best score. This is called the X-drop rule. Figure 55.4 shows it for a hit in a stretch of DNA where a subject is related to the query for 100 bases and unrelated after that. While the extension runs through the related stretch, matches outnumber mismatches, and the score climbs, with small dips at each mismatch. Once it runs past the end into unrelated sequence, mismatches dominate, the score falls, and the extension stops when it is \(X\) below the best.








Figure 55.4: The X-drop rule, here with X = 20. The extension score climbs while the two sequences are related, and falls once the extension runs past the end of the related stretch. The extension stops when the score is X below the best seen so far (orange dot), and the alignment is trimmed back to where the best score was (blue dot).





The result is a high-scoring segment pair, or HSP. For our small query and subject, extending the hit at the start of the diagonal gives an HSP with a score of 34 that covers the whole query:


TGCATGCCAGTTACGGATCAAG
||||||| ||||||| ||||||
TGCATGCAAGTTACGCATCAAG


Extending every one of the 15 hits gives only 5 different HSPs. All hits on the main diagonal grow into the same HSP, and the chance hits on other diagonals grow into short HSPs with low scores. Most of the extension work is therefore wasted, a point the improved BLAST of 1997 takes up.

title: 55  BLAST
text:
Word size and threshold
A BLAST search spends most of its time extending hits, so the number of hits decides how fast it is. It can only find a relative that contains at least one hit, so the number of hits in relatives determines how sensitive it is: how distant relatives it can still find. Both depend on the word size and the threshold.
First, how many chance hits should we expect? In random DNA, each base is one of four with equal chance, so a given word of length \(w\) matches a given position with probability \(1/4^w\). A query with about \(m\) words, scanned against a database with about \(n\) positions, gives about
\[\frac{m \, n}{4^w}\]
random hits. Each extra base in the word divides that number by four. A 1,000-base gene searched against the human genome with \(w = 11\) gives about 740,000 random hits, each of which would be extended. With \(w = 28\), the word size of megablast, it gives about 0.00004: none at all.
For DNA, the real BLAST does not use neighborhoods. It looks only for exact words, so the threshold is always the top score, and it controls the trade-off with word size alone. That also saves work: the neighborhood of a word at the top score is just the word itself, so BLAST never has to try all \(4^w\) possible words, which is about 4 million for \(w = 11\) and more than a billion for \(w = 15\).
To see the trade-off, take a random query of 300 bases and a relative of it, in which about a third of the bases have been replaced by random ones, hidden between two random stretches. Figure 55.5 shows the dot plots for three word sizes.








Figure 55.5: Dot plots of a random 300-base query against a 900-base subject that holds a relative of the query in its middle third, for three word sizes. With w = 6, the relative is buried in random hits. With w = 16, only a short piece of its diagonal is left.





With \(w = 6\), the diagonal of the relative is there, but it is surrounded by random hits, and each one would be extended. With \(w = 11\), the random hits are nearly gone, and the diagonal still shows. With \(w = 16\), the random hits are gone, but so is most of the diagonal: only one short piece of it survives, where the relative happens to share a long identical stretch with the query.
One example is not much to go on, so Figure 55.6 counts properly. The database here is a million random bases, with 60 relatives of a 400-base query hidden in it, 20 each at three divergence levels. For each word size, the figure shows the number of random hits, and how many of the 20 relatives at each level got at least one hit on their own diagonal. One hit is all BLAST needs to find a relative, because one hit is enough to start an extension.








Figure 55.6: Speed and sensitivity for exact words of different sizes, searching a 400-base query against a million random bases with 60 hidden relatives. Left: the number of random hits that must be extended, with the expected number as a dashed line. Right: how many of the 20 relatives at each level of identity got at least one hit.





The two panels tell the whole story. As $ w$ goes from 7 to 15, the number of random hits drops from 24,014 to 0, and the time spent extending drops with it. But the relatives disappear too, and the most distant ones disappear first. Nearly all 78% identical relatives appear at every word size. The 55% identical ones are all found with \(w = 7\), but only 5 with \(w = 11\) and 0 with \(w = 15\), because a sequence that differs from the query at almost every other base rarely contains a long unbroken identical stretch.
No setting is best for everything. It depends on what you are looking for, which is why NCBI offers several versions of nucleotide BLAST (see Choosing an algorithm). megablast uses \(w = 28\) and is very fast, but it finds only nearly identical sequences. The standard blastn uses \(w = 11\). And you can set the word size yourself on the BLAST page, under Algorithm parameters.






NoteProtein search



Proteins are different in two ways. First, there are 20 amino acids rather than four bases, so even a three-letter word is rare: a given word matches a random position only once in \(20^3 = 8000\). Second, related proteins often have similar amino acids in the same place rather than identical ones, like a leucine (L) where the other has an isoleucine (I). Exact words would miss those, so protein BLAST uses short, three-letter words and makes them sensitive to local neighborhoods.
To score words, BLAST uses the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix (Henikoff and Henikoff, 1992), which you gave the protein aligner in the Biopython chapter. Unlike the DNA scores, BLOSUM62 gives different pairs of amino acids very different scores. A Q against an E scores 2, because glutamine and glutamate are similar, while a W against a G scores -2. So the neighborhood of PQG at \(T = 13\) includes PQG itself, which scores 18, but also PDG, PEG, PHG, PKG, PMG, PNG, PRG, PSG: every word where the middle amino acid is one that BLOSUM62 considers a reasonable stand-in for glutamine. A protein neighborhood depends on which letters differ, and how many.
For proteins, the word size stays at 3, and the threshold \(T\) trades speed for sensitivity. To measure it, take a random protein query of 150 amino acids, and a database of about 100,000 amino acids with ten relatives hidden in it, in which about half the amino acids have been replaced:



Threshold
Hits
Random hits
Relatives found




\(T = 11\)
44,460
44,041
10 of 10


\(T = 13\)
17,064
16,757
10 of 10


\(T = 15\)
5,972
5,765
10 of 10



Raising \(T\) cuts the number of hits, and with it the work, several times over. The relatives hold up much better, because a relative half of whose amino acids are unchanged contains many words that score well, and it only needs one of them to be found.



Step 4: could it be chance?
Search a big enough database with any query, and you will find something that scores well, just by chance. So BLAST must tell you how surprised you should be by a score. It does so with the E-value: the number of alignments with at least this score you would expect to find by chance alone in a database of random sequences of this size.
For ungapped alignments, there is a formula for it, found by Samuel Karlin and Stephen Altschul (Karlin and Altschul, 1990):
\[E = K \, m \, n \, e^{-\lambda S}\]
Here \(S\) is the score, \(m\) is the query length, \(n\) is the total database length, and \(K\) and \(\lambda\) are constants that depend on the scoring table. For BLOSUM62 without gaps, \(\lambda \approx 0.318\) and \(K \approx 0.134\).
Read the formula as a story. The \(e^{-\lambda S}\) part makes \(E\) shrink very quickly as the score goes up: a high score is unlikely to happen by chance. The \(m \, n\) part makes \(E\) grow with search size: the more places you look, the more chance hits you will find. So the same alignment gets a different E-value depending on which database you searched, as Figure 55.7 shows.








Figure 55.7: E-value against score for a 300-letter protein query, with BLOSUM62 and no gaps, in databases of three sizes. Every 10-point score increase divides the E-value by about 24. Making the database 100 times larger moves the line up by a factor of 100.





As an example, the two short proteins MSHWEKLNGCAPRTYIDVQKFGEMLW and TTGAPNSHWEKINGCAPKTFIDLRSAQPLE share a stretch that the toy BLAST finds and extends into this HSP:


SHWEKLNGCAPRTYIDVQ
SHWEKINGCAPKTFIDLR


It scores 89. Found in a database of 200 million amino acids, it would have an E-value of 3.7e-04: you would expect an alignment this good by chance in about one search out of 2,700.
Because \(K\) and \(\lambda\) differ between scoring tables, you can’t compare raw scores across them. BLAST therefore also reports a bit score, \(S' = (\lambda S - \ln K) / \ln 2\), which puts every scoring system on the same scale. With bit scores, the formula becomes simply \(E = m \, n \, 2^{-S'}\). The same formula holds for DNA, with \(K\) and \(\lambda\) taken from the DNA scores.

Exercise 55-1
AI: Explainer
Ask the assistant what the E-value of a BLAST hit means, and whether an E-value of 0.01 means there is a 1% chance that the hit is a coincidence. Then work it out yourself from the formula: what happens to the E-value of the same alignment if the database were ten times smaller, and what does that tell you about whether the E-value can be a property of the hit alone? Decide whether the assistant’s explanation holds up, and note in your logbook what it got right and what it got wrong.






TipShow the answer





With a database ten times smaller, \(n\) is ten times smaller, so \(E\) is ten times smaller too: 0.001 instead of 0.01, for the same two sequences aligned in the same way. The E-value is therefore a property of the hit and the search. It says how many alignments at least this good you would expect from random sequences in a search of this size. For small values, that is close to the probability of getting at least one such alignment by chance anywhere in the search (\(1 - e^{-E}\), which is 0.00995 for \(E = 0.01\)). That is not the same as the probability that this particular hit is a coincidence, which also depends on how many real relatives the database holds. An explanation that says “a 1% chance this hit is random” and stops there has skipped the part about the size of the search.

title: 55  BLAST
text:
Gapped BLAST
Seven years after the first paper, the same group published a new BLAST for proteins (Altschul et al., 1997) that was about three times faster and at least as sensitive. It changed two things. The authors measured where the original BLAST spent its time. Most of it went to Step 3, extending hits, and almost all of those extensions led nowhere: a random match in a random place, extended a few letters until the X-drop rule stopped it. You saw a different kind of waste in Step 3: when an alignment is good, it contains many hits on the same diagonal, and each one extends into the same HSP.
Both observations point to the same fix. An alignment worth finding is usually long enough to contain more than one hit. A random hit, by contrast, is rarely accompanied by another nearby hit on the same diagonal. So the new BLAST only extends when it finds two hits on the same diagonal that do not overlap and are no more than \(A\) letters apart. The paper used \(A = 40\). This is the two-hit method, and the two hits together are sometimes called a paired seed. To find them, BLAST sorts the hits by diagonal, \(j - i\), and looks at neighboring hits along each diagonal.
Requiring two hits means fewer extensions, but it also risks missing alignments that only have one hit. To win back that sensitivity, the authors lowered the threshold \(T\) from 13 to 11. As the table in the section on protein search shows, that means bigger neighborhoods and many more hits. But since only pairs of hits trigger an extension, the number of extensions still drops sharply. On the protein database from that section, the original one-hit BLAST with \(T = 13\) extends 17,064 hits and finds 10 of the 10 relatives. The two-hit BLAST with \(T = 11\) starts from 44,460 hits, but extends only 2,250 paired seeds, and finds 10 relatives. Figure 55.8 shows why. Only about one random hit in 21 has a nearby partner on its diagonal, so most are never extended. A relative, by contrast, has hits along its diagonal, and many come in pairs.








Figure 55.8: Hits of the protein query at T = 11 in a stretch of the database that holds one relative, whose diagonal is shaded blue. Gray dots are hits. Orange dots are paired seeds: the second of two hits on the same diagonal, no more than 40 letters apart. Only the orange dots are extended. Along the diagonal of the relative, they form a line, while elsewhere only a few random hits happen to pair up.






Exercise 55-2
SOLO
A protein search with word size 3 has produced these hits, written as (position in query, position in subject):
(5, 25)   (14, 34)   (30, 10)   (60, 80)   (61, 81)   (70, 50)   (102, 122)
Find the diagonal of each hit. Then, for each diagonal, sort its hits by query position and look at each pair of neighbors. Which pairs trigger an extension with \(A = 40\)? Remember that the two hits must not overlap. For each pair that does not trigger one, say which condition it fails.






TipShow the answer





Five hits lie on diagonal 20 (query positions 5, 14, 60, 61 and 102) and two on diagonal −20 (query positions 30 and 70). On diagonal 20, the hits at 5 and 14 are 9 apart, which is at least 3 and at most 40, so they trigger an extension. The hits at 14 and 60 are 46 apart, too far. The hits at 60 and 61 are only 1 apart, so their words overlap, and they count as one clue. The hits at 61 and 102 are 41 apart, just too far. On diagonal −20, the hits at 30 and 70 are exactly 40 apart, which is allowed. So 2 extensions start, from the hits (14, 34) and (70, 50).



The original BLAST found only ungapped alignments. If a related sequence had an insertion, BLAST would report two separate HSPs, one on each side of it, each with a weaker score and a worse E-value than the whole alignment deserved.
The 1997 BLAST adds gaps, but without paying for a full Smith-Waterman alignment. When an ungapped extension reaches a score high enough to be interesting, BLAST picks a point in the middle of the best part of that HSP and starts a gapped alignment from there, spreading outward in both directions. It fills the alignment table like Smith-Waterman, with one difference: it uses the X-drop idea again and stops filling cells whose score has dropped too far below the best seen so far. In practice, it only fills in a narrow band around the diagonal, which is a tiny part of the full table. Only a handful of HSPs per search ever get that far, so the gapped step costs little.
Gapped alignments come at a statistical cost. The formula for the E-value was proven only for ungapped alignments, but it fits gapped ones too, with different values of \(\lambda\) and \(K\). Those values were found by aligning huge numbers of random sequences and measuring, and BLAST keeps a table of them for each combination of substitution matrix and gap scores. For BLOSUM62 with an affine gap score of 11 to open and 1 to extend, the default for blastp, \(\lambda\) is 0.267 and \(K\) is 0.041, as the search in the Biopython BLAST section reports. That is why you can choose only from a fixed menu of gap scores on the BLAST website. The same paper also introduced PSI-BLAST, which you will meet among the variants below.

title: 55  BLAST
text:
BLAST at NCBI
Today’s BLAST at NCBI, called BLAST+ (Camacho et al., 2009), is a descendant of the 1997 version. Go to blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and look at the start page while you read this section. It offers five basic programs, and which one you need depends on two questions: is your query DNA or protein, and is the database DNA or protein?









Program
Query
Database
What is compared




blastn
DNA
DNA
DNA with DNA


blastp
protein
protein
protein with protein


blastx
DNA
protein
the query translated in all six reading frames, with proteins


tblastn
protein
DNA
the protein with the database translated in all six reading frames


tblastx
DNA
DNA
the query translated in six frames, with the database translated in six frames



Why translate at all, when you could compare DNA with DNA? Because proteins change more slowly than the DNA that codes for them. The genetic code has several codons for most amino acids, so the DNA of two related genes can drift apart while their proteins stay much the same. Comparing at the protein level finds relatives that blastn would miss. You saw the DNA side of this in Figure 55.6: once a relative is only about half identical at the DNA level, exact DNA words rarely find it. The six reading frames are the three ways to split a DNA sequence into codons on each of the two strands, as in the ORF project (Chapter 46). Because tblastx compares each of the six frames of the query with each of the six frames of every database sequence, it makes 36 comparisons per sequence pair, which is why it is by far the slowest of the five.

Choosing an algorithm
Once you pick nucleotide or protein BLAST on the website, the page lets you choose among algorithm variants under Program Selection. They differ in how they find hits, which is Step 1 and Step 2 above.
For nucleotide BLAST, the choice is a speed-sensitivity trade-off from earlier in this chapter. megablast finds sequences that are nearly identical to yours, like the same gene in another person or a closely related species. It is the fastest because it requires an exact match of 28 bases before it extends anything (Zhang et al., 2000), and long words produce very few random hits. blastn is the classic version and uses 11-base words. It is slower but finds more distant relatives. discontiguous megablast is meant for comparing genes across more distantly related species. Its words are spaced seeds: it looks at, say, 11 positions spread out over a window of 16 or more bases, and ignores the positions in between (Ma et al., 2002). If the ignored positions are the third positions of codons, where mutations often do not change the amino acid, the seed still matches two genes whose DNA differs at many third positions. It gets some of the sensitivity of short words with the few random hits of long ones.
For protein BLAST, the variants differ more. blastp is the standard protein search, essentially the 1997 algorithm. Quick BLASTP is an accelerated version that NCBI recommends when you expect your relatives to share at least half their amino acids with your query. PSI-BLAST (position-specific iterated BLAST, from the same 1997 paper) runs blastp and then builds a new scoring table from the significant hits it found. In that table, each position of your query gets its own scores, so a position that is always a glycine among the relatives scores very high for glycine and low for everything else, while a position where the relatives vary is more forgiving. It then searches again with that table, and repeats. Each round can find relatives too distant for the previous round to see. The danger is that a single unrelated sequence that sneaks into the table drags in its own relatives in the next round, so you must look at what is added each round. PHI-BLAST only reports alignments that contain a pattern you give it, such as a known active-site motif (Zhang et al., 1998). DELTA-BLAST builds a position-specific scoring table like PSI-BLAST, but gets it from a database of known protein domains rather than your own search (Boratyn et al., 2012). That often finds distant relatives in a single round.


Choosing a database
The database menu matters as much as the program because the E-value depends on database size, and because you can only find what is in it. For proteins, nr (non-redundant) holds nearly every protein sequence NCBI has, ClusteredNR groups very similar sequences in nr together so that you get one hit per group rather than a hundred near-identical ones, refseq_protein holds NCBI’s curated reference sequences, swissprot holds the hand-curated UniProt/Swiss-Prot entries, and pdb holds proteins with a known 3D structure. For DNA, there is a large nucleotide collection along with more specialized databases, such as RefSeq transcripts and genomes. The menu changes as NCBI reorganizes its data, so read each database’s description before you choose one.
NCBI also offers specialized tools built on BLAST, which you find further down the start page. Primer-BLAST designs PCR primers and checks that they only match where you want them to. IgBLAST analyzes antibody and T-cell receptor sequences. SmartBLAST gives a quick overview of the best protein matches. If you tick Align two or more sequences on any of the search pages, you can compare your query directly with sequences you paste in, without searching a database at all.

Exercise 55-3
SOLO
For each situation below, decide which program you would use, and for nucleotide searches, which algorithm. Write down your answer and a one-sentence reason for each before you open the answer. Base the reasons on what you have seen in this chapter, in particular Figure 55.6.

You have a gene from a mouse and want to find the same gene in other mammals, where you expect the DNA to be about 85% identical.
You want to find the same gene in fish, where you expect the DNA to be much less similar.
You have sequenced a stretch of DNA from an unknown bacterium and want to know whether it codes for a known protein.
You have a protein from a fruit fly and want to find the genes in a newly sequenced, not yet annotated, mosquito genome that code for something similar.
You have a PCR product and want to check that it matches the human gene you meant to amplify.







TipShow the answer





Mouse to other mammals: blastn, or discontiguous megablast. At 85% identity, a related gene still has plenty of unbroken stretches of 11 bases, like the 78% identical relatives in Figure 55.6, which were found at every word size. Stretches of 28 identical bases are rarer, so megablast may miss parts of the gene.
Mouse to fish: compare proteins instead. Translate the gene and use blastp against fish proteins, or tblastn against fish genomes. At low DNA identity, exact DNA words rarely hit (the 55% identical relatives in the figure), while the protein is far better conserved. discontiguous megablast is the nucleotide option if you must stay with DNA.
Unknown bacterial DNA: blastx, which translates your DNA in all six frames and searches the protein database.
Fly protein against an unannotated mosquito genome: tblastn, which translates the genome in all six frames. No annotated mosquito proteins exist to search with blastp yet.
PCR product against the human gene: blastn with megablast. You expect a nearly identical match, and long words make it fast.





Exercise 55-4
SOLO
Go to the BLAST website, choose Protein BLAST, and search with the human FOXP2 protein from the Biopython chapter against the swissprot database. You can paste its accession, NP_683698.2, into the query box. Before you press the button, predict what the list of hits will look like: which proteins will be at the top, and will there be other proteins than FOXP2 further down? When the results come in, look at the E-value, percent identity, and bit score of the hits. Where in the list does the percent identity suddenly drop, and what kind of proteins come after that point? Why are most of the E-values reported as 0?






TipShow the answer





The top of the list is FOXP2 from other species: other primates, mouse, rat, and further down, a frog. These are orthologs, the same gene in different species, and they are more than 90% identical to the human protein. Then the identity drops to around 60%, and the hits are FOXP1, FOXP4, and FOXP3. These are paralogs: other members of the same gene family in the same and other species, which arose by gene duplication long before the species split. The E-values are reported as 0 because they are too small to print: with bit scores in the hundreds, the number of alignments this good you would expect among random sequences is so tiny that BLAST rounds it to 0. The first hit, human FOXP2 itself, is not 100% identical, because our protein is isoform IV, made from transcript variant 4, and the Swiss-Prot entry is the canonical isoform. The alignment has gaps where one isoform has a stretch of amino acids the other lacks. The next section shows the same search done from Python.

title: 55  BLAST
text:
Biopython BLAST
You can run the same searches from Python. The function Blast.qblast in Biopython sends your sequence to NCBI’s BLAST servers. You give it the BLAST program, the database, and your sequence. An NCBI search takes at least a minute, and when many people use the servers, it can wait in the queue much longer. NCBI also asks that you send no more than one search every ten seconds. So you save the result to a file and work with the file from then on:
from Bio import Blast

Blast.email = "your.name@post.au.dk"   # use your own address

stream = Blast.qblast("blastp", "swissprot", protein, hitlist_size=20)
with open("data/foxp2_blastp.xml", "wb") as f:
    f.write(stream.read())
stream.close()
Here protein is the FOXP2 protein sequence as a string. The "wb" opens the file for writing bytes rather than text, because the stream from NCBI delivers bytes. The result is an XML file, which Blast.read turns into Python objects. The record holds one Hit for each database sequence that BLAST found, and you loop over it like a list. Each Hit holds one or more HSPs, which are the alignments between your sequence and that database sequence, and each HSP has its statistics in a dictionary called annotations:
blast_record = Blast.read("data/foxp2_blastp.xml")
for hit in blast_record:
    hsp = hit[0]
    identity = 100 * hsp.annotations["identity"] / hsp.length
    print(hit.target.id, hsp.annotations["evalue"], round(identity, 1),
          hit.target.description[:40])

title: 56  DNA sequence divergence across time
text:
Every time a cell divides, it copies its DNA, and sometimes the copy has a mistake. Most mutations that get passed on through generations are neutral: they change the DNA without changing anything the organism depends on. Because neutral mutations arise at a roughly steady rate and selection neither favors nor removes them, they pile up in a lineage like the ticks of a clock. This is the molecular clock. If you know how fast the clock ticks, you can read off how long it has been running from the number of differences it has left behind.






Figure 56.1: A molecular clock. Following one lineage from the past to the present, the sequence collects mutations (stars) at a rate of about \(5 \times 10^{-10}\) per base per year in humans. Three of the 17 bases have changed, so the clock has been running for about \(\frac{3/17}{5 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 353\) million years.



Figure 56.1 shows the idea for a single lineage. In practice, we never have the ancestral sequence. We have two sequences from two living species, as in Figure 56.2. Since the two species split from their common ancestor \(T\) years ago, each lineage has been collecting substitutions for \(T\) years, so the two sequences are separated by \(2T\) years of evolution. If \(K\) is the number of substitutions per site that separate them and \(r\) is the substitution rate per site per year, then
\[
r = \frac{K}{2T} \qquad \text{and so} \qquad T = \frac{K}{2r}.
\]






Figure 56.2: Two species that split \(T\) years ago. Each lineage has collected substitutions for \(T\) years (red), so the sequences we compare are separated by \(2T\) years of evolution.



The two sequences in Figure 56.2 differ at 3 of their 12 sites, so \(K = 0.25\). With \(r = 5 \times 10^{-10}\), that gives \(T = 0.25 / (2 \times 5 \times 10^{-10}) = 250\) million years. The calculation assumes that every substitution leaves a visible difference, and that is only true for closely related sequences. The rest of this section is about what happens when it is not.

A model of DNA evolution




Distant past  GCTTGCACGA GCTTGAACGA GCTTGAACGA GCTCGAACGA GCTCGAACGA GCACGAACGT GCATGAACGT GCATGAACGT GCATGGACGT GCATGGACGT  Present


Figure 56.3: Six substitutions in a ten-base sequence, read from top to bottom. Only three differences between the first and last sequence are visible. The fourth base changed from T to C and back to T, and the sixth changed twice: first to A, then to G.



Figure 56.3 follows one sequence through time. Six substitutions happen, but comparing the first sequence with the last shows only three differences. One site changed and then changed back, which leaves no trace, and another changed twice, which looks like one change. The longer the sequences have been evolving apart, the more often a site is hit more than once, and the more the observed proportion of differences underestimates the number of substitutions that actually happened. To correct for this, we need a model of how bases change over time: a way to compute the probability that a site holds base \(x\) now, given that it held base \(y\) at time \(t\).
Think of a single site. Let \(p_A(t)\) be the probability that it holds an A at time \(t\), and likewise for the other three bases. Over a short time \(\Delta t\), two things can change \(p_A\). If the site is an A, it may mutate to another base at rate \(\mu_A\). If it is another base \(x\), it may mutate to A at rate \(\mu_{xA}\). So
\[
p_A(t+\Delta t) = p_A(t) - p_A(t)\, \mu_A \Delta t + \sum_{x \neq A} p_x(t) \, \mu_{xA} \Delta t,
\]
where \(\mu_A = \sum_{x \neq A} \mu_{Ax}\) is the total rate at which an A turns into something else. The same equation holds for each of the four bases. Collecting the four probabilities in a vector,
\[
\mathbf{p}(t) = (p_A(t),\ p_C(t),\ p_G(t),\ p_T(t)),
\]
all four equations can be written as one:
\[
\mathbf{p}(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{p}(t) + \mathbf{p}(t)\,Q\,\Delta t,
\]
where \(Q\) is the rate matrix. Its entry in row \(x\) and column \(y\) is the rate at which base \(x\) mutates to base \(y\), and each diagonal entry is minus the total rate of leaving that base, so that every row sums to zero:
\[
Q = \begin{pmatrix}
-\mu_A & \mu_{AC} & \mu_{AG} & \mu_{AT} \\
\mu_{CA} & -\mu_C & \mu_{CG} & \mu_{CT} \\
\mu_{GA} & \mu_{GC} & -\mu_G & \mu_{GT} \\
\mu_{TA} & \mu_{TC} & \mu_{TG} & -\mu_T
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Different models of DNA evolution are different choices for the twelve rates in \(Q\).


Jukes-Cantor model
The simplest model, from Jukes and Cantor (1969), assumes that every base mutates to each of the three others at the same rate, \(\alpha\). With \(\alpha = \mu / 4\), the rate matrix is
\[
Q = \begin{pmatrix}
-3\alpha & \alpha & \alpha & \alpha \\
  \alpha & -3\alpha & \alpha & \alpha \\
  \alpha & \alpha & -3\alpha & \alpha \\
  \alpha & \alpha & \alpha & -3\alpha
\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
-\frac{3\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} \\
\frac{\mu}{4} & -\frac{3\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} \\
\frac{\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} & -\frac{3\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} \\
\frac{\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} & \frac{\mu}{4} & -\frac{3\mu}{4} \\
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Letting \(\Delta t\) shrink towards zero turns the equation for \(\mathbf{p}\) into a differential equation, and for this simple \(Q\) it can be solved by hand. The solution gives the probability of going from one base to another in time \(t\), as a matrix \(P(t)\) whose entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is the probability that a site holding base \(i\) holds base \(j\) at time \(t\) later:
\[
P(t) = \left(
\begin{array}{cccc}
\frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} e^{-t\mu}  & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} \\[1.5ex]
\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} \\[1.5ex]
\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} \\[1.5ex]
\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-t\mu} & \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} e^{-t\mu} \\
\end{array}
\right)
\]
At \(t = 0\), the diagonal entries are 1, and the others are 0: nothing has had time to change. As \(t\) grows, every entry approaches \(\frac{1}{4}\): after a very long time, the site is equally likely to hold any base, whatever it started as.
It is more useful to measure time by the number of substitutions that have actually happened per site, which we call \(\nu\). A site leaves its base at the rate \(\frac{\mu}{4} + \frac{\mu}{4} + \frac{\mu}{4}\), so
\[
\nu = \frac{3\mu}{4}\, t \quad \implies \quad t\mu = \frac{4}{3}\nu,
\]
and the transition probabilities become
\[
  P_{ij}(\nu) =
  \begin{cases}
    \, \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} e^{-4\nu/3} & \text{if } i = j\\[0.5ex]
    \, \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-4\nu/3} & \text{if } i \neq j
  \end{cases}
\]
When we compare two sequences, \(\nu\) is the number of substitutions per site along the whole path from one sequence back to their common ancestor and forward to the other, which is the \(K\) of the molecular clock. A site differs between the two sequences if it has ended up as any of the three other bases, so the expected proportion of sites that differ is
\[
p = 3\times \bigg(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} e^{-4\nu/3} \bigg)= \frac{3}{4} - \frac{3}{4} e^{-4\nu/3}.
\]
Figure 56.4 shows what this means. For a short time, \(p\) grows almost in step with the number of substitutions, along the dashed line. Then it bends away, because more and more new substitutions land on sites that already differ. Eventually \(p\) levels off at \(\frac{3}{4}\): two unrelated sequences still agree at a quarter of their sites, just by chance.











(a) With substitutions accumulating at \(10^{-8}\) per site per year between the two sequences. The dashed line is what we would see if no site were ever hit twice. Three times as much time only a little more than doubles the proportion of differences.











(b) Against the number of substitutions per site, \(\nu\). However many substitutions have happened, the proportion of differences never exceeds 0.75 (dashed line).







Figure 56.4: The proportion of sites that differ between two sequences under the Jukes-Cantor model.



We observe \(p\), but we want \(\nu\). Solving the equation for \(\nu\) gives the Jukes-Cantor correction:
\[
\nu = -\frac{3}{4} \ln\Big(1-\frac{4}{3}p\Big)
\]
For small \(p\), the correction hardly matters: \(p = 0.05\) gives \(\nu = 0.052\). For large \(p\), it matters a lot: \(p = 0.5\) gives \(\nu = 0.82\), so the observed differences hide more than a third of the substitutions. The corrected \(\nu\) is what goes into the molecular clock as \(K\).
Figure 56.5 turns the correction into time. Because the curve in Figure 56.4 flattens out, the estimated time shoots up as \(p\) approaches 0.75, and a small error in \(p\), which you always have with sequences of limited length, becomes a huge error in the time. Sequences that differ at more than about two-thirds of their sites are in the twilight zone, where DNA comparisons can no longer tell how long ago two sequences diverged, or even whether they are related at all. This is one reason we compare distant relatives at the protein level, where the twilight zone comes much later.








Figure 56.5: Time estimated with the Jukes-Cantor correction from the observed proportion of differences, with substitutions accumulating at \(10^{-8}\) per site per year between the two sequences. In the gray twilight zone, a small change in the observed proportion gives a very different time.







Kimura’s 2-parameter model
The four bases fall into two chemical classes. A and G are purines, with two rings, and C and T are pyrimidines, with one. A mutation that swaps a purine for a purine or a pyrimidine for a pyrimidine is a transition. One that swaps a purine for a pyrimidine, or vice versa, is a transversion. Transitions are chemically easier, and although there are twice as many kinds of transversion, transitions are observed about twice as often as all transversions together. The Jukes-Cantor model ignores this.
Kimura (1980) gave transitions their own rate, \(\alpha\), and transversions another, \(\beta\), as in Figure 56.6. Each base has one transition partner and two transversion partners, so with the bases in the order A, C, G, T, the rate matrix is
\[
Q = \begin{pmatrix}
-2\beta-\alpha & \beta & \alpha & \beta \\
  \beta & -2\beta-\alpha & \beta & \alpha \\
  \alpha & \beta & -2\beta-\alpha & \beta \\
  \beta & \alpha & \beta & -2\beta-\alpha
\end{pmatrix}.
\]








Figure 56.6: Kimura’s 2-parameter model. Transitions (solid blue) swap a purine for a purine or a pyrimidine for a pyrimidine and happen at rate \(\alpha\). Transversions (dashed orange) swap a purine for a pyrimidine and happen at rate \(\beta\).





As with the Jukes-Cantor model, solving this model gives a correction formula. If \(s\) is the observed proportion of sites that differ by a transition, and \(v\) the proportion that differ by a transversion, the number of substitutions per site is
\[
d_{K2P} = - \frac{1}{2} \ln \big( 1 - 2s - v\big) - \frac{1}{4} \ln \big( 1 - 2v\big).
\]
When transitions and transversions do happen at the rates the Jukes-Cantor model assumes (\(\alpha = \beta\)), the two formulas give about the same answer. When transitions are more common, as they nearly always are, the Kimura correction is larger because frequent transitions saturate sooner and hide more substitutions.
