title: 57  Scoring matrices
text:
From counts to scores
To align two proteins, you need a score for every pair of amino acids that can end up in the same column, as in the pairwise alignment chapter. With 20 amino acids, that is a \(20 \times 20\) table, and since a pair scores the same regardless of which sequence each amino acid is in, there are 210 different scores to decide. The scores should be positive for pairs that appear together in related proteins more often than by chance, and negative for pairs that appear together less often. A “same or different” score, as we used for DNA, cannot do this. In real proteins, an isoleucine is often replaced by a valine, which is similar in size and also hydrophobic, while a tryptophan is almost never replaced by a glycine. The most widely used tables of this kind are the BLOSUM matrices (Henikoff and Henikoff, 1992), and BLOSUM62 is the default in BLAST (see the BLAST chapter).
The BLOSUM matrices are counted from real proteins. The data are the BLOCKS database: more than 2,000 ungapped multiple alignments of the conserved regions of more than 500 protein families. Because the blocks have no gaps, each column is a set of amino acids assumed to descend from the same ancestral amino acid. Gaps therefore play no part in the matrix, and the gap scores for protein alignment are chosen separately.
The idea is to go through every column of every block, look at every pair of sequences, and count which two amino acids they have in that column. One problem is that some protein families include many nearly identical sequences, which would dominate the counts and tell us mostly about pairs that have barely had time to change. So before counting, we cluster the sequences in each block: a sequence joins a cluster if it is at least \(X\) percent identical to any sequence already in it. A sequence in a cluster of \(n\) sequences then gets weight \(1/n\), so each cluster counts as a single sequence, and pairs within a cluster are not counted at all. For every pair of sequences in different clusters, add the product of their weights to the count \(f_{ij}\) for the two amino acids \(i\) and \(j\) they have in that column. Sum these counts over all columns of all blocks, then convert them into scores as described below.
The threshold \(X\) gives the matrix its name: \(X = 62\) gives BLOSUM62, \(X = 80\) gives BLOSUM80, and \(X = 45\) gives BLOSUM45. A high threshold merges few sequences, so counts are dominated by close relatives, and the matrix suits comparisons of closely related proteins. A low threshold merges away close relatives, so only distantly related pairs are counted, and the matrix suits distant relatives.
The counts are first turned into the observed frequency of each pair,
\[
q_{ij} = \frac{f_{ij}}{\sum_{i \le j} f_{ij}},
\]
where the sum runs over every pair once, so that A–S and S–A are the same pair. From these, the background frequency of each amino acid is its share of all the members of all the pairs. An amino acid paired with itself is both members of the pair, and one paired with another is half of it:
\[
p_i = q_{ii} + \sum_{j \ne i} \frac{q_{ij}}{2}.
\]
If amino acids were paired at random, the pair \(i\)–\(j\) would turn up with the expected frequency
\[
e_{ij} = \begin{cases} p_i^2 & \text{if } i = j \\ 2 p_i p_j & \text{if } i \ne j, \end{cases}
\]
where the 2 is there because \(i\) can be in either sequence. The score compares what was observed with what chance would give, as a log-odds score:
\[
s_{ij} = \log_2 \frac{q_{ij}}{e_{ij}}.
\]
A pair seen twice as often as chance scores 1, one seen half as often scores −1, and one seen exactly as often as chance scores 0. Because the logarithm has base 2, the score is measured in bits. The published matrix scales the scores and rounds them to whole numbers. BLOSUM62 is in half-bits, \(S_{ij} = \mathrm{round}(2 \log_2 (q_{ij}/e_{ij}))\), while some other matrices, such as BLOSUM50, are in thirds of a bit.
To see the steps in action, take a tiny block of five sequences and three columns, and skip the clustering:
Five sequences make 10 pairs in each column, so 30 pairs in all. The background frequencies come out as \(p_A = 0.533\), \(p_C = 0.267\), \(p_S = 0.133\) and \(p_W = 0.067\), and the four pairs that occur get these scores:
Two things in the table may surprise you. C–W scores higher than C–C, and A–S scores higher than A–A, even though identical amino acids are paired more often. Scores measure how surprising a pair is compared with chance, and S and W are rare, so seeing them at all in a pair is surprising. Pairs that never occur, like A–C, have \(q = 0\), which gives them a score of minus infinity. With so little data, the matrix is odd. The real BLOCKS data hold enough pairs that every combination is seen.

title: 57  Scoring matrices
text:
Reading the matrix
Figure 57.1 shows the whole of BLOSUM62. The diagonal is all positive, from 4 to 11: an amino acid is most often replaced by itself, meaning it is not replaced at all. Rare amino acids score highest when they match, because a match between two rare amino acids is unlikely by chance: tryptophan with tryptophan scores 11 and cysteine with cysteine 9, while alanine with alanine scores 4. Off the diagonal, the scores run from −4 to 3, and the positive ones form small groups of chemically similar amino acids: isoleucine, leucine, valine and methionine; phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan; lysine and arginine; aspartate and glutamate.








Figure 57.1: The BLOSUM62 matrix, with the amino acids ordered so that chemically similar ones sit next to each other. Blue cells are pairs seen in related proteins more often than by chance, orange cells less often.





The log-odds form makes an alignment score meaningful. Consider two ways an aligned pair of sequences could have arisen. Either they are related, so each column is a pair drawn with the observed frequencies \(q_{ij}\), or they are unrelated, so each amino acid is drawn independently with the background frequencies. The score of an ungapped alignment is the sum of the scores of its columns, and a sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product. So the total score in bits is
\[
S = \log_2 \frac{P(\text{alignment} \mid \text{related})}{P(\text{alignment} \mid \text{unrelated})}.
\]
Every extra bit doubles how much more likely the alignment is if the sequences are related, and every half-bit unit in BLOSUM62 multiplies it by \(\sqrt{2}\). Here is an ungapped alignment of two short peptides, scored with BLOSUM62:
M K T A Y I A K
M K S A F V A R
5 5 1 4 3 3 4 2   total 27
Every column scores positive: four identities, and four substitutions between similar amino acids. The relationship goes both ways, too. Any score matrix, even one made up by hand, implies a set of target frequencies \(q_{ij} = p_i p_j \, 2^{s_{ij}}\): the frequencies of pairs in related sequences that it is best at finding (Altschul, 1991).
Two numbers summarize a matrix. The relative entropy \(H = \sum_{i \le j} q_{ij} \, s_{ij}\) is the average score per column in true relatives: how much information each aligned pair carries about whether two sequences are related. The expected score \(E = \sum_{i \le j} e_{ij} \, s_{ij}\) is the average score per column for unrelated sequences. As you saw for local alignment, \(E\) must be negative for local alignment to work, or random sequences would build up long high-scoring alignments (Karlin and Altschul, 1990). For BLOSUM62, \(H = 0.6979\) bits and \(E = -0.5209\) bits (Henikoff and Henikoff, 1992). A higher BLOSUM number gives a higher \(H\): more information per column, so shorter alignments can be detected, but only between close relatives.

title: 57  Scoring matrices
text:
Using the matrix
You do not have to type in the matrix. Biopython has BLOSUM62 and many other matrices built in, and you look up a score with two amino acids, as in the Biopython chapter:
from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices

blosum62 = substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62")
print(blosum62["W"]["W"])
print(substitution_matrices.load())   # the names of all the matrices
Besides the 20 amino acids, the matrix has rows for B (aspartate or asparagine), Z (glutamate or glutamine), X (any amino acid), and * (a stop codon). A substitution matrix plugs straight into the Needleman-Wunsch and Smith-Waterman algorithms of Chapter 53 in place of the simple match and mismatch scores. You must choose gap scores separately, usually by trial and error. The default in blastp` is BLOSUM62 with an affine gap score of 11 to open a gap and 1 to extend it.

title: 57  Scoring matrices
text:
PAM, for contrast
Before BLOSUM, the standard matrices were the PAM matrices of Margaret Dayhoff and colleagues (Dayhoff et al., 1978). They were built differently. Dayhoff took closely related proteins, at least 85% identical, built evolutionary trees, and counted the substitutions along the branches. From those counts, she made the PAM1 matrix, which describes the changes expected after one accepted substitution per 100 amino acids. Matrices for longer distances were made by applying PAM1 repeatedly, as a model like the one in A model of DNA evolution does over time: PAM250 is PAM1 applied 250 times, then converted to log-odds scores. So the PAM matrices for distant relatives are extrapolated from close relatives, while each BLOSUM matrix is counted directly from sequences at its distance.
The numbers run in opposite directions. A high PAM number means distant relatives, while a high BLOSUM number means close ones. Roughly, PAM250 corresponds to BLOSUM45, PAM160 to BLOSUM62, and PAM120 to BLOSUM80. When Henikoff and Henikoff compared them in database searches, BLOSUM62 found relatives better than the PAM matrices, and it became the default in BLAST.

Choosing a matrix
For most searches, BLOSUM62 is a good choice. If you are looking for close relatives, BLOSUM80 is better, and for distant relatives, BLOSUM45. NCBI also bases its advice on the length of the query, because a short query gives a short alignment, and a short alignment can only stand out from chance if each column carries a lot of information: PAM30 for queries shorter than 35 amino acids, PAM70 for 35 to 50, BLOSUM80 for 50 to 85, and BLOSUM62 for anything longer.
Figure 57.2 shows why the three BLOSUM matrices suit different distances. The matrices are published in different units, BLOSUM62 in half-bits and the other two in thirds of a bit, so the figure converts every score to bits to make them comparable. Going from BLOSUM45 to BLOSUM80, the diagonal gets darker blue and the rest of the matrix darker orange. On average an identity is worth 2.3 bits in BLOSUM45 and 3.1 bits in BLOSUM80, while a substitution costs 0.45 bits in BLOSUM45 and 0.98 bits in BLOSUM80. BLOSUM80 was counted from close relatives, where substitutions are rare, so it treats every substitution as strong evidence against a relationship. BLOSUM45 was counted from distant relatives, where substitutions are common, so it forgives them. The relative entropy grows accordingly, from 0.3795 bits per column for BLOSUM45 to 0.6979 for BLOSUM62 and 0.9868 for BLOSUM80.








Figure 57.2: BLOSUM45, BLOSUM62 and BLOSUM80 side by side, with the amino acids in the same order as in Figure 57.1. Every score is converted to bits and colored on the same scale in all three panels, so the same color means the same evidence for or against a relationship.





Every substitution matrix rests on two simplifications. It assumes that each position in a protein evolves on its own, and that the same scores apply at every position. Neither is true. An amino acid buried in the core of a protein faces very different constraints than one on its surface. The matrices work well anyway, which says more about how useful a simple model can be than about how proteins evolve. Even the matrix itself is not quite what it was meant to be: the BLOSUM62 that everyone uses was computed with a mistake in the clustering code, and the corrected matrix found relatives slightly worse (Styczynski et al., 2008).

title: 58  Project: HIV sub-groups
text:
Compute the similarity of two sequences
This chapter is a programming project where you will put your new programming skills to use analyzing an HIV DNA sequences.
You have now been introduced to all the programming rules you will see in this course. You now know all the building blocks required to write any program – and I do mean any. The reason why computer geeks are good at what they do is not that they know some incomprehensible secrets. It is because they practiced, a lot. With practice, the simple rules you know now will let you write anything from first-person shooter games over jumbo jet autopilots to scripts for simple problems in bioinformatics. In the last three chapters, we will train your ability to solve bioinformatics problems by putting together all the things you have learned.
The programming project in this chapter deals with DNA sequences from HIV viruses. There are two types of HIV: HIV-1, which is by far the most common, and HIV-2, which is mostly found in West Africa. HIV-1 vira are divided into groups M, N, O, and P. The most important group M (for major) is one primarily responsible for the global epidemic. Group M is further divided into subtypes A, B, C, D, F, G, J, K, and CRFs. In this project we will look at sequences from the subtypes A, B, C, and D. You have multiple database sequences for each of these four subtypes and you have one unknown sequence from a patient that you need to assign to either subtype A, B, C or D. To do this you will have to write a program that predicts the subtype of the unknown sequence. How cool is that?
Begin by downloading the project. Open your instructing machines folder in VS Code. Then open a terminal (Terminal > New Terminal from the top menu) and run this command:
That puts the hivproject project folder straight into the projects folder inside your course folder, beside your notebooks.
If that fails, you can always click “Download project” in the top right corner of the page. This downloads a zip file to your Downloads folder that you need to then unpack and move into the projects folder of your student folder yourself.
You write your code in the file called hivproject.py. In the terminal, navigate to the project folder and run your code in the usual way:
To test the functions as you complete each one, you use pytest to run the project test suite in test_hivproject.py using this command:
Either way you get a folder called hivproject with these files in it:
Now open each file in VScode and have a look at what is in the data files. (Do not change them in any way and do not save them after viewing. If VScode asks you if you want to save it before closing, say no.) How many sequences are there in each file?
The project is divided into the following parts:
Make sure you read the entire exercise and understand what you are supposed to do before you begin!
We need to compare our unknown HIV sequence to all the HIV sequences of known subtypes. That way we can identify the sequence of a known subtype that is most similar to your unknown sequence. We will then assume that our unknown sequence has the same subtype as this sequence. To accomplish this we first need to write some code that compares two sequences so we can compare our HIV sequence to each of the other HIV sequences.

title: 58  Project: HIV sub-groups
text:
Compare two sequences
Write a function sequence_similarity that takes two arguments:

A string which is a DNA sequence.
A string of the same length as argument one, which is also a DNA sequence.

The function must return:

A float, which is the proportion of bases that are the same in two DNA sequences.

Example usage:
sequence_similarity('AGTC' 'AGTT')
should return 0.75.
Start out defining your function like this:
def sequence_similarity(seq1, seq2):
    # your code here...
Remember that range(len(seq1)) generates the numbers you can use to index the string seq1. You can use those numbers as indexes to look up positions in both strings. You will need a for-loop in your function and a variable that keeps track of how many similarities you have seen as you iterate through the sequences.


Compare aligned sequences
All sequences, including the unknown sequence, are from the same multiple alignment. This ensures that sequence positions match up across all sequences but also means that a lot of gap characters ('-') are inserted. To compute similarities between such sequences you need to make function much like seqeuence_similarity that does not consider sequence positions where both bases are a gap ('-') characters. In other words, you must not only count the number of characters that are the same, you also need to count how many alignment columns that are "-" for both sequences. E.g. the following mini alignment has five such columns and four columns where the bases are the same. So in the following alignment, the similarity is 0.8 (4/5):
A-CT-A
A-CTTA
Write a function alignment_similarity that takes two arguments:

A string which is a DNA sequence with gap characters.
A string of the same length as argument one, which is also a DNA sequence with gap characters.

The function must return:

A float, which is the proportion of bases that are the same in two DNA sequences.

alignment_similarity('A-CT-A', 'A-CTTA')
should return 0.8.






NoteHint





Use an if-statement to test if the two characters at some index are equal to '-' in both sequences. You can use an expression like this:
seq1[i] == '-' and seq2[i] == '-'



Once your function has computed both the number of identical bases and the number of alignment columns that are not both '-', you can have it return the similarity as the ratio of the two.

title: 58  Project: HIV sub-groups
section: Read the HIV sequences into your program
text:
Read the HIV sequences into your program
To use your alignment_similarity function to assess similarity between your unknown sequence and the sequences of known subtype, you need to read the sequences into your program. Here is a function that will read the sequences from one of the files you downloaded into a list:
def read_data(file_name):
    f = open(file_name)
    sequence_list = list()
    for line in f:
        seq = line.strip()
        sequence_list.append(seq)
    f.close()
    return sequence_list
You can use that function to read the unknown sequence into your program:
unknown_list = read_data('unknown_type.txt')
In this case, the list only contains the one unknown HIV sequence in unknown_type.txt.
You also need to load the typed HIV sequences into your program. Here is a function that returns a dictionary in which the keys are subtypes ('A', 'B', 'C' and 'D') and each value is a lists of sequences with that subtype:
def load_typed_sequences():
    return {'A': read_data('subtypeA.txt'),
            'B': read_data('subtypeB.txt'),
            'C': read_data('subtypeC.txt'),
            'D': read_data('subtypeD.txt') }
If you use the function like this:
typed_data = load_typed_sequences()
then you can access the list of sequences of subtype A like this: typed_data['A'].

section: Compute maximum similarity to each subtype
text:
Compute maximum similarity to each subtype
To predict the subtype of the unknown HIV sequence you need to compare the unknown sequence to all the sequences of each of the different subtypes. The subtype of the sequence with the highest similarity to your unknown sequence is then our predicted subtype (or our best guess).
Write a function get_max_similarities that takes two arguments:

The function must return:

A dictionary, in which keys are strings representing each subtype ('A', 'B', 'C', and 'D') and values are floats representing the maximum similarity between the unknown sequence and the sequences of a subtype. subtypeA_similarities = get_similarities(unknown_list[0], typed_data['A'])

title: 58  Project: HIV sub-groups
text:
Identify the HIV subtype
Now for the grand finale! You ultimately want to be able to write code like this:
unknown_list = read_data('unknown_type.txt')
typed_data = load_typed_sequences()
subtype = predict_subtype(unknown_list[0], typed_data)

So all you need now is the predict_subtype function.
Write a function predict_subtype that takes two arguments:

A string, which is your unknown HIV sequence.
A dictionary, like the one returned by load_typed_sequences.

The function must return:

A string of length one (either 'A', 'B', 'C', or 'D') representing the predicted subtype of your unknown HIV sequence.

The function should use get_max_similarities to compute the dictionary of max similarities and then extract from that dictionary the key with the highest value (similarity). So the function must return 'A' if the unknown sequence is most similar to a sequence of subtype A, 'B' if the unknown sequence is most similar to a sequence of subtype B and so on.

title: 59  Recursion
text:
What happens when you call a function
A function that calls itself sounds like a joke or a disaster. It is neither. It is the sharpest tool in this book, and learning it will teach you what a function really is.
Before we do anything alarming, let us go back over something you already know. Read this and run it:
%%sandbox
def greeting(name):
    salute = "Hello"
    return salute + " " + name


message = greeting("Mogens")
print(message)
Now walk through it one line at a time, top to bottom:
Nothing new there. But notice how much of it you are now taking for granted: that the body is a template, not a thing that runs when you write it; that calling it creates a fresh little world every single time; that the world is thrown away when the function returns.
Hold on to those three facts. They are all you need for what follows.

title: 59  Recursion
text:
Python reads def greeting(name): and the indented block under it. It does not run them. It just remembers that there is a function called greeting, and what its body looks like.
Python reaches message = greeting("Mogens"). Now it runs the body — a temporary little world springs into being, with name holding "Mogens" and, a line later, salute holding "Hello".
The return hands back "Hello Mogens", and the whole expression greeting("Mogens") is substituted for that string. The temporary world evaporates. name and salute are gone.
message is assigned "Hello Mogens".

title: 59  Recursion
text:
Recursion
Apparently complicated problems can often be solved recursively, if the whole problem can be split into smaller problems of exactly the same kind.
That is the whole idea. Read it again, because the important word is identical. Not “smaller problems”. Smaller problems of the same kind, so that whatever solves the big one also solves the small ones.
And if the same thing solves both, you only have to write it once — and then have it call itself.

title: 59  Recursion
text:
Factorial
Here is the classic example. The factorial of 4, written \(4!\), is
\[4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1\]
Look at that product and squint. Inside it, tucked on the right, sits \(3 \times 2 \times 1\), which is \(3!\). And inside that sits \(2 \times 1\), which is \(2!\). So:
\[4! = 4 \times 3!\]
which is the same as saying that if you already knew the factorial of 3, computing the factorial of 4 would be one multiplication of work. And you would know the factorial of 3 if you knew the factorial of 2. And so on.
Two lines describe the whole thing:
\[\text{Recursion:} \quad f(x) = x \times f(x-1)\]
\[\text{Basis:} \quad f(1) = 1\]
The first line says how to make the problem smaller. The second says when to stop. You need both. The first one alone is a machine for making ever-smaller problems that never actually get solved; it is the basis that eventually gives a real answer for the whole tower of calls to be built on.

Exercise 59-1
SOLO
Write a Python function called factorial that takes one argument and computes the factorial recursively. You have everything you need: def, if, return, and the two lines of maths above. The table in the margin is there so you can check yourself — start with factorial(4), where you know the answer must be 24.
Do this one yourself before you read on or ask anyone, human or otherwise. It is four lines long, and it is the most valuable four lines you will write this term.
Here is one solution:

%%sandbox
def factorial(x):
    if x == 1:
        return 1
    return x * factorial(x-1)

Read it against the two lines of maths. The if is the basis. The last line is the recursion. Nothing else is in the function, and nothing else needs to be there.
If your reaction to that last line is “but you cannot call factorial inside factorial, it is not finished yet” — good. That reaction is exactly what we are going to take apart.

title: 59  Recursion
text:
Why it works
Go back to the three facts I asked you to hold on to.
A function definition is a template. When Python reads def factorial(x):, it does not run anything; it just remembers the body. So there is no problem writing a call to factorial inside the body — by the time that line actually runs, the definition is long finished.
And calling a function creates a fresh temporary world. So when factorial(3) reaches return x * factorial(x-1) and calls factorial(2), a brand new world appears, with its own x holding 2. The outer x is untouched. It sits there, patiently waiting for its multiplication to finish.
Figure 59.1 shows all of it at once for factorial(3). Each box is one call, one temporary world, with its own x.






Figure 59.1: Three calls to factorial, one inside the next. Each box is a temporary world with its own x. The innermost one hits the base case and returns a real number, and then the answers are multiplied on the way back out.



Follow it downwards first. factorial(3) cannot return until it knows factorial(2). factorial(2) cannot return until it knows factorial(1). And factorial(1) does not need anybody: x == 1 is True, so it returns 1 straight away.
Now follow it back up, and read it as pure reduction, the way you have been reading expressions since Chapter 14. In the middle box, factorial(1) is substituted for 1, so return 2 * factorial(1) becomes return 2 * 1, which reduces to 2. In the outer box, factorial(2) is substituted for 2, so return 3 * factorial(2) becomes return 3 * 2, which reduces to 6.
Substitution and reduction. That is all recursion is. You already knew how to do this. Recursion is a good test of whether you really understand functions. If a recursive call looks impossible to you, it is because you haven’t fully understood that a function definition is a template, and every call builds a fresh temporary world from that template; each world has its own variables and its own patiently waiting, half-finished expressions.

Exercise 59-2
SOLO
Add a print to the top of the function so you can watch the worlds being created:

%%sandbox
def factorial(x):
    print("starting factorial({})".format(x))
    if x == 1:
        return 1
    return x * factorial(x-1)


print(factorial(4))

Before you run it: how many lines will be printed, and in what order will they appear relative to the final answer? Decide, then run.


Exercise 59-3
SOLO
Now watch them close down again. Predict the entire output of this, in order, before you run it:

%%codelens
def factorial(x):
    print("entering factorial({})".format(x))
    if x == 1:
        print("basis: returning 1")
        return 1
    result = x * factorial(x-1)
    print("factorial({}) returns {}".format(x, result))
    return result


print(factorial(4))

If your prediction was wrong, do not just re-read the output until it looks reasonable. Draw the boxes of Figure 59.1 for factorial(4) on paper and walk through them with your finger.


Exercise 59-4
SOLO
Try this:

%%sandbox
def factorial(x):
    if x == 1:
        return 1
    return x * factorial(x-1)


print(factorial(100))

and then this:

%%sandbox
def factorial(x):
    if x == 1:
        return 1
    return x * factorial(x-1)


print(factorial(1000))

One of them prints an absurdly long number. The other doesn’t print anything at all. Instead, you get an error you haven’t seen before. Read it. Python is telling you that there is a limit to how deep this can go — each of those temporary worlds takes up room, and Python refuses to stack up more than about a thousand of them.
That limit is not a flaw. It is a smoke alarm. A recursion that runs away is one of the easiest bugs to write, and this is Python catching it for you.


Exercise 59-5
SOLO






ImportantSpot the bug



The factorial above is deliberately fragile. It is not a typo; it is a missing case.


What do you think factorial(0) does? Decide first. Then run it, and explain the error you get in terms of the base case. Then fix the function so that factorial(0) returns 1, which is what mathematicians have agreed \(0!\) should be. There is more than one way to fix it, and they are all one character or one line.

title: 59  Recursion
text:
Divide and conquer
Factorial is the traditional first example, but it is a slightly dishonest one, because a for-loop would have done the job just as well. Here is a problem where a loop will not save you.
A tree is one of those things you can only really describe in terms of itself. Look at Figure 59.2. At the very top sits a node. Two things hang under it. Each of those is either a leaf — the end of the line, with a name on it — or another node with two more things hanging under it.






Figure 59.2: A tree with five leaves, and the same tree written as nested lists. Each colored pair of brackets is one node in the tree.



In Python, we can write a tree as nested lists. The tree in Figure 59.2 is:

%%sandbox
tree = [[['A', 'C'],'B'],['E', 'D']]

Take a moment with the colors in the figure. Each pair of matching brackets in the nested list is one node in the drawing, and the colors pair them up. The red brackets form the outermost list and the top node. Inside the red list are two things: the blue list and the magenta list — which is exactly what the drawing shows hanging under the red node.

Exercise 59-6
SOLO
Look at the nested list and only the nested list, without looking at the drawing. Which two things are inside the blue list? Which two are inside the orange list? Then check yourself against Figure 59.2.


Exercise 59-7
SOLO
Write the nested list for a tree where the top node has a leaf 'X' on the left and, on the right, a node with leaves 'Y' and 'Z'. Then draw it.

title: 59  Recursion
text:
Counting the leaves
Now the question: how many leaves does a tree have?
You could try to write a loop. Go on, think about it for a minute. How many levels of nested loops would you need? The answer depends on how deep the tree is, and you don’t know how deep the tree is. Even if you did, you would need to rewrite the program for every new tree. This is where loops run out.

Exercise 59-8
SOLO
Answer these three questions on paper before writing any code:

How could you find the number of leaves on a tree using recursion?
How can you split the problem into smaller problems of exactly the same kind?
What is the base case that has an obvious, immediate answer?

Look at Figure 59.3 if you get stuck. It shows the answer written next to every node: 1 at each leaf, and at every other node the sum of the two numbers below it.






Figure 59.3: The same tree, with the number of leaves written at each node. Every node’s number is the sum of the two numbers below it.





Exercise 59-9
SOLO
Write a function called count that takes a tree and returns the number of leaves on it. Test it on [[['A', 'C'],'B'],['E', 'D']], where you know from Figure 59.3 that the answer must be 5.
One hint, and it is the only one you get. You need to tell a leaf from a node. A leaf is a string and a node is a list, so you can test for it like this:
if type(tree) is str:
    # what to do when it is a leaf...
Here is one solution:

%%sandbox
def count(tree):
    if type(tree) is str:
        return 1
    return count(tree[0]) + count(tree[1])


tree = [[['A', 'C'],'B'],['E', 'D']]

print(count(tree))

Three lines. Compare them with the three questions you answered on paper: the if is the base case, and the last line splits into two identical smaller problems.
Notice that the last line calls count twice. No rule says a recursive function may only call itself once, and that is what makes recursion so much more powerful than a loop here. Each call branches into two more, and the branching follows the shape of the tree without you ever having to know how deep it goes.
Figure 59.4 shows every call that happens when you run it. The colors match Figure 59.2: each call gets exactly the part of the tree that its node is responsible for.






Figure 59.4: Every call made by count on the example tree. The call tree has the same shape as the tree itself.



That is the thing worth staring at. You did not write the shape of that diagram. The tree did. Your function only ever described what to do at one node, and the shape came out of the data.


Exercise 59-10
SOLO
Predict what happens with each of these, then run them:

%%sandbox
def count(tree):
    if type(tree) is str:
        return 1
    return count(tree[0]) + count(tree[1])


print(count('A'))
print(count(['A', 'B']))
print(count([['A', 'B'], ['C', 'D']]))

The first one is worth a moment’s thought. Is a single leaf a tree?


Exercise 59-11
SOLO
Add a print to count so it announces every call, like this:

%%sandbox
def count(tree):
    print("count({})".format(tree))
    if type(tree) is str:
        return 1
    return count(tree[0]) + count(tree[1])


print(count([[['A', 'C'],'B'],['E', 'D']]))

Run it and compare the printed lines with Figure 59.4. Do they come out in the order you expected? Which call finishes first, and which finishes last?


Exercise 59-12
Open the assistant in the browser, give it the count function and the tree, and ask it to list every call that gets made, in the order they are made. Do not run anything yet. Write its answer down.
Now run the version with the print in it and compare, line for line. Assistants are good at recursion in general and surprisingly slippery about the exact order of calls in a particular one. Where did it agree with the machine, and where did it not?
Put the result in your logbook. This is the rule of the whole course in one exercise: the assistant predicts, the machine proves.


Exercise 59-13
SOLO
Write a function that returns a list of all the leaves on a tree, rather than the number of them. On the example tree it should return ['A', 'C', 'B', 'E', 'D'].
The same hint applies for telling a leaf from a node. And one more: count returned a number and added the two results together with +. Your function returns a list. What does + do to two lists?


Exercise 59-14
SOLO
Write a function that returns the depth of a tree — the number of steps from the top node down to the deepest leaf. A single leaf has depth 0. On the example tree, the answer is 3.
You will need the built-in function max, which takes two numbers and returns the larger of them. Predict the answer for ['A', 'B'] before you run anything.

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
What is a regular expression?
A regular expression is a tiny program that describes a pattern in text. The re module is the machine that runs it.
You already know how to look for a piece of text inside a string. The in operator tells you whether it is there, .find tells you where, and .count tells you how many times. If you want to know whether a DNA sequence contains a site for the restriction enzyme EcoRI, which cuts DNA wherever it sees GAATTC, that is all you need:
Now take the enzyme HinfI. It cuts at GANTC, where N means any base. 'GANTC' in dna will not help you, because it looks for a real letter N, and there is none in your DNA. You could check GAATC, GACTC, GAGTC and GATTC one at a time, but that gets old fast. The TATA box, a short sequence found in many promoters, has the consensus TATAWAW, where W means A or T. That is four strings to check. And if you want to find a poly-A tail, a run of As of any length, there is no list of strings you can write down at all.
What you need is a way to describe a pattern rather than spell out every string that fits it. That is what a regular expression is. It is a small language of its own, with its own grammar, and it does exactly one thing: it instructs a little machine to look for text that fits a description. A course called Instructing Machines could hardly leave it out.
A regular expression (people often just say regex) is a description of a set of strings. The pattern GAATTC describes exactly one string. The HinfI site GANTC describes four DNA strings, one for each base in the middle. And the pattern for a poly-A tail describes infinitely many: A, AA, AAA, and so on forever. You write the description, and the re module checks text against it.
That lets you ask four kinds of questions, and you will meet all of them in this chapter:
The idea is older than most programming languages. The mathematician Stephen Kleene invented the notation in the 1950s, and in the late 1960s Ken Thompson built it into a text editor, and later into the command-line tool grep, whose name stands for globally search for a regular expression and print. Since then regular expressions have found their way into almost every programming language and text editor. What you learn here also works, with small differences in the details, in R, on the command line, and in the search box in VS Code (click the .* button).
When you write a for-loop that walks along a sequence looking for something, Python carries out every single step of it: take the next index, cut out a slice, compare it, add one to a counter, go round again. Python reads and carries out your instructions one at a time, and each of those small steps costs time.
When you call re.search, none of that walking happens in Python. The re module translates your pattern into a compact set of instructions for a regular expression engine: a small, specialized machine, written in the much faster language C, whose only job is to run patterns over text. Engines like it have been tuned and optimized by programmers for decades, because searching text is something computers are asked to do all the time. Your one line of Python hands the whole job over, and the engine does the walking.

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Searching: is there anything in this text that fits the description, and where?
Validating: does the whole string fit? Is this string a DNA sequence at all?
Extracting: which pieces fit, and what are the parts inside them? Pull the chromosome, start and end out of chr7:114086327-114693772.
Replacing: swap everything that fits for something else, for instance to strip the numbers and spaces out of a sequence copied from a GenBank file.





Exercise 60-1
SOLO
The code below counts the EcoRI sites in a sequence of 1.8 million bases twice: first with a for-loop that compares every six-base slice to GAATTC, then with re.findall, which you will meet properly in Finding all of them. The time module from the standard library lets you read the clock before and after each one. Do both ways find the same number of sites? And which do you think is faster, and by how much: twice as fast, ten times, a hundred times? Decide before you run it.

%%sandbox
import re
import time

dna = 'ATGCGAATTCTTAGCCAT' * 100000

start = time.time()
count = 0
for i in range(len(dna) - 5):
    if dna[i:i+6] == 'GAATTC':
        count = count + 1
print('Loop:', count, 'sites in', time.time() - start, 'seconds')

start = time.time()
count = len(re.findall('GAATTC', dna))
print('re:  ', count, 'sites in', time.time() - start, 'seconds')

On my laptop, the engine is about forty times faster than the loop. Your numbers will be different, and they will change a little every time you run the cell, but the engine wins by a wide margin. On a whole genome that is the difference between waiting a second and waiting a minute.
One fair warning before you get carried away: string methods such as .find and .count are written in C too, so for exact text like GAATTC they are just as fast as re. The engine earns its keep when you are looking for a pattern rather than a fixed string, which is what the rest of this chapter is about. And speed is never an excuse for a pattern nobody can read (see When not to use them).
Regular expressions live in the re module, which is part of Python’s standard library (see Modules in Python’s Standard Library). You do not need to install anything, you just import it.


Exercise 60-2
SOLO
Read the code below and run it:

%%sandbox
import re

dna = 'CCGAATTCATGGATCCTTGAATTCGG'
re.search('GAATTC', dna)

re.search takes two arguments: the pattern you are looking for and the string you are looking in. It found an EcoRI site and handed you back a match object. When it is displayed, it tells you two things: match='GAATTC' is the text it found, and span=(2, 8) is where it found it. The span works just like a slice: dna[2:8] is 'GAATTC'.
Notice that the sequence contains two EcoRI sites, and re.search only told you about the first one. It stops searching as soon as it finds something. You will see how to get all of them in Finding all of them.
A match object is an object like any other, and it has methods. .group() gives you the text that matched, .start() the index where the match begins and .end() the index just after it ends.


Exercise 60-3
SOLO
Decide what you think each of the three lines will print before you run the code. Then run it to check.

%%sandbox
import re

dna = 'CCGAATTCATGGATCCTTGAATTCGG'
match = re.search('GGATCC', dna)
print(match.group())
print(match.start())
print(match.end())



Exercise 60-4
SOLO
The enzyme NotI cuts at GCGGCCGC. There is no NotI site in our sequence. What do you think re.search returns when it finds nothing? Decide, then run it.

%%sandbox
import re

dna = 'CCGAATTCATGGATCCTTGAATTCGG'
match = re.search('GCGGCCGC', dna)
print(match)

When there is no match, re.search returns None. You met None in the chapter on functions, and you met truthiness even earlier: a match object counts as True and None counts as False. That is not an accident. It means you can put a search straight into an if statement:

%%sandbox
import re

dna = 'CCGAATTCATGGATCCTTGAATTCGG'
match = re.search('GGATCC', dna)
if match:
    print('BamHI site at index', match.start())
else:
    print('No BamHI site')



Exercise 60-5
SOLO
What happens if you skip the if and call .start() on the result of a search that found nothing? Predict whether you get an error, and if so which one, before you run the code below.

%%sandbox
import re

dna = 'CCGAATTCATGGATCCTTGAATTCGG'
match = re.search('GCGGCCGC', dna)
print(match.start())

Read the last line of the traceback carefully. None has no .start() method, and Python says so. You will see this error a lot when you start using regular expressions, and now you know what it means: a search found nothing, and the code carried on as if it had.
So far, the patterns have been ordinary strings, and re.search('GAATTC', dna) does nothing that dna.find('GAATTC') could not do. Time to change that.

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Metacharacters
Most characters in a pattern just match themselves: a G matches a G. A handful of characters are special. They are called metacharacters, and they are what makes a regular expression more than a string.
The first one is the dot. A . matches any single character. That is exactly the N in the HinfI site GANTC:

%%sandbox
import re

re.search('GA.TC', 'TTGACTCAA')


Exercise 60-6
SOLO
For each of the four searches below, decide whether it finds a match and, if it does, what text it matches. Write your four answers down before you run the code.

%%sandbox
import re

print(re.search('GA.TC', 'GATTCGAGTC'))
print(re.search('GA.TC', 'GATC'))
print(re.search('GA.TC', 'GA.TC'))
print(re.search('GA..C', 'AAGAATTCAA'))

The second one is the one people get wrong: the dot has to match exactly one character. It cannot match nothing.


Character classes
The dot is often too generous. In the TATA box consensus TATAWAW, the W is not any base, it is A or T. Square brackets let you list the characters allowed at a single position. [AT] matches one character that is either an A or a T. This is called a character class:

%%sandbox
import re

promoter = 'GCGCTATAAAAGGCGC'
re.search('TATA[AT]A[AT]', promoter)

A character class always matches exactly one character, however many characters you list inside the brackets. A few more tricks go inside the brackets:

[A-Z] is a range: any uppercase letter. [0-9] is any digit.
[^GC] with a ^ first is the opposite: any character that is not G or C.

Some classes are so common that they have their own shorthand. \d matches any digit, like [0-9]. \s matches any whitespace (a space, a tab or a newline). \w matches any word character: a letter, a digit or an underscore.





pattern
matches one




G
G


.
any character


[AT]
A or T


[A-Z]
uppercase letter


[^GC]
anything but G, C


\d
digit


\s
whitespace


\w
letter, digit or _




Exercise 60-7
SOLO
Predict what each line prints, then run the code to check.

%%sandbox
import re

print(re.search('[^ACGT]', 'ACGTACGNACGT'))
print(re.search(r'\d', 'chromosome 7'))
print(re.search(r'\s', 'FOXP2 gene'))
print(re.search('[GC][GC][GC]', 'ATGCATGGCATT'))




Raw strings
You probably noticed that the patterns with a backslash in them were written as r'\d' instead of '\d'. In the chapter on files, you saw that a backslash already means something in an ordinary Python string: '\n' is a single newline character, not a backslash followed by an n. Regular expressions use backslashes too, and the two uses get in each other’s way. Putting an r in front of the string makes it a raw string, where Python leaves every backslash alone and passes it on untouched to the re module.
Some patterns happen to work without the r and some silently do something else, and you do not want to have to remember which. Always write your patterns as raw strings. Just trust me on that one.


When you mean an actual dot
What if you want to match a character that happens to be a metacharacter, like a real dot? You put a backslash in front of it. \. matches a dot and nothing else, \( matches an opening parenthesis, and so on. This is called escaping the character.

Exercise 60-8
SOLO






ImportantSpot the bug



The pattern in the cell below is wrong on purpose. Your job is to find out how.


The code below is supposed to report which lines mention the FOXP2 transcript NM_148900.4. Only the first line does. The third line mentions NM_14890014, a completely different accession number. Run the code and see that it reports the third line anyway. Explain why, then fix the pattern so that only the first line matches.

%%sandbox
import re

lines = ['Reads aligned to NM_148900.4',
         'Reads aligned to NM_148900.3',
         'Reads aligned to NM_14890014']
for line in lines:
    print(line, re.search('NM_148900.4', line))

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Repeating patterns
So far, every piece of a pattern matched exactly one character. Quantifiers change that. A quantifier goes right after the thing it applies to and says how many times it may repeat:

+ means one or more times,
* means zero or more times,
? means zero or one time (i.e., it is optional),
{3} means exactly three times, and {2,5} means between two and five times.






pattern
means




A+
one or more A


A*
zero or more A


A?
zero or one A


A{3}
exactly three A


A{2,5}
two to five A


A{4,}
four or more A



Here is the poly-A tail that no list of strings could describe:

%%sandbox
import re

mrna = 'AUGGCCUAAGCGAAAAAAAAAAAA'
re.search('A+', mrna)

Hmm. It matched a single A, the one in AUGGCC. That is correct, though: A+ means one or more As, and the very first A in the string is one or more As. The search always reports the leftmost place where the pattern fits. If you want a real tail, say what you mean by one, for instance at least six As:

%%sandbox
import re

mrna = 'AUGGCCUAAGCGAAAAAAAAAAAA'
re.search('A{6,}', mrna)

When a quantifier has a choice, it takes as many characters as it can. Once it found six As, it kept going and took all twelve. Quantifiers are greedy.

Exercise 60-9
SOLO
Predict exactly what text each search matches before you run the code. The quantifier applies only to the single character right in front of it.

%%sandbox
import re

print(re.search('CA*G', 'TTCAAAGTT'))
print(re.search('CA*G', 'TTCGTT'))
print(re.search('CA+G', 'TTCGTT'))
print(re.search('colou?r', 'the color of the gel'))
print(re.search('[ACGT]{3}', 'NNATGNN'))



Exercise 60-10
SOLO
Greed can surprise you. The pattern below is meant to find a stretch that starts with ATG and ends with the stop codon TAA. The sequence contains two TAAs. Which one do you think the match ends at? Decide, then run it.

%%sandbox
import re

re.search('ATG.+TAA', 'ATGAAATAAGGGTAA')

The .+ gobbled up as much as it could and only gave characters back when it had to, so the match ends at the last TAA. If you put a ? after a quantifier, it becomes lazy and takes as few characters as it can instead. Try changing the pattern to 'ATG.+?TAA' and run it again.
(Before you get ideas: finding real open reading frames takes more than this, because the stop codon has to be in the same reading frame as the start codon. You will do it properly in the ORF project.)

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Anchors
Two metacharacters match no character at all. They match a position. ^ matches the start of the string and $ matches the end. Together they let you insist that a pattern describes the whole string and not just some piece of it.

Exercise 60-11
SOLO
The pattern ^[ACGT]+$ reads from the start, one or more of A, C, G or T, then the end. Decide which of the four strings it matches before you run the code.

%%sandbox
import re

for seq in ['ACGTTGCA', 'ACGTNGCA', 'acgt', '']:
    print(repr(seq), re.search('^[ACGT]+$', seq))

Note that ^ means two different things: outside square brackets it is start of the string, and as the first character inside them it is not. Same symbol, different job.


Exercise 60-12
SOLO
Write a function is_dna that takes a string and returns True if it consists only of the uppercase letters A, C, G and T, and False otherwise. A function that returns True or False should return exactly those values and not a match object or None, so you need one small extra step after the search. These lines should all print True:
print(is_dna('ACGTTGCA') == True)
print(is_dna('ACGTNGCA') == False)
print(is_dna('acgt') == False)

%%sandbox
import re

# Your code here

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Finding all of them
re.search stops at the first match. To get every match, use re.findall, which returns a list of the matched strings:

%%sandbox
import re

dna = 'TTGACTCAAGATTCCGAGTCA'
re.findall('GA.TC', dna)

That is three HinfI sites, and you can see which base sits in the middle of each. A list of strings does not tell you where they are, though. For that, use re.finditer. It gives you the match objects one at a time, so it works with a for-loop just like a list or a file does:

%%sandbox
import re

dna = 'TTGACTCAAGATTCCGAGTCA'
for match in re.finditer('GA.TC', dna):
    print(match.group(), 'at', match.start())


Exercise 60-13
SOLO
How many times do you think ATA occurs in ATATATA? Count them yourself by sliding your finger along the string. Then predict what re.findall returns, and run the code.

%%sandbox
import re

re.findall('ATA', 'ATATATA')

You should have counted three, at index 0, 2 and 4. re.findall found two. Once the regular expression machine has found a match, it continues searching right after that match, so matches never overlap. The .count method on strings works the same way. For restriction sites that rarely matters, but for short repeated motifs it can quietly give you the wrong count.


Exercise 60-14
AI: Explainer
Ask the assistant how to make re.findall (or re.finditer) also find overlapping matches. It will most likely give you a pattern containing something you have not seen, such as (?=...). Do not accept it until you can say in your own words what each character in the pattern does, so keep asking about the parts you cannot explain. Then let the machine settle it: run the suggested code on 'ATATATA' and on 'AAAAA' with the pattern AA, and compare both results with the count you get by sliding your finger along the string. Write in your logbook whether the assistant’s explanation agreed with what the code actually did.

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Groups: pulling out the pieces
Often you do not just want to know that a pattern matched; you want to pull pieces out of the text it matched. Wrap a piece of the pattern in parentheses, and the match object remembers what that piece matched. The parenthesized pieces are called groups, and they are numbered from 1 in the order of their opening parentheses.
Genomic coordinates are often written like chr7:114086327-114693772: the chromosome, a colon, the start position, a dash and the end position. Here is a pattern that takes it apart:

%%sandbox
import re

region = 'chr7:114086327-114693772'
match = re.search(r'(\w+):(\d+)-(\d+)', region)
print(match.group(1))
print(match.group(2))
print(match.group(3))

match.group() with no argument (or with 0) still gives you the whole match. match.groups() gives you all the groups at once as a tuple.

Exercise 60-15
SOLO
Using region and the pattern from above, compute the length of the region by subtracting the start from the end. Before you run your code, decide what type match.group(2) returns. If your first attempt gives you an error, read it, and remember what you know about converting between types.

%%sandbox
import re

region = 'chr7:114086327-114693772'
match = re.search(r'(\w+):(\d+)-(\d+)', region)

# Your code here

When the pattern has groups, re.findall changes what it returns. Instead of a list of whole matches, you get a list of tuples with one string per group. That fits nicely with the tuple unpacking you learned in Chapter 22:

%%sandbox
import re

text = 'Regions: chr7:114086327-114693772, chrX:1000-2000 and chr2:500-900.'
for chrom, start, end in re.findall(r'(\w+):(\d+)-(\d+)', text):
    print(chrom, int(end) - int(start))



Exercise 60-16
SOLO

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Replacing and splitting
re.sub finds every match of a pattern and replaces it with something else. It takes three arguments: the pattern, the replacement and the string. This is very handy for cleaning up data.
Here are the first three lines of the sequence part of that same GenBank file, exactly as they appear in it. Each line starts with a number, and the bases come in blocks of ten, separated by spaces:

%%sandbox
import re

block = '''
        1 acagacatga aagctaaccg aggacttgag agactcaaac tggtgctttt gtctctctct
       61 ctctgtcttt ctctctctca cacacacact cacacactca cacacatgca cacacacaca
      121 tacacacaca caaaaatgaa gcacttactt tagaaagatt atggtaagca tgctggctca
'''
seq = re.sub(r'[\d\s]', '', block).upper()
print(seq)
print(len(seq))

The pattern [\d\s] matches any single digit or whitespace character, and each one is replaced by the empty string, i.e., deleted. Then .upper() makes it look like the DNA you are used to.

Exercise 60-17

Look at the second line of the block. It contains a long stretch of CA repeated over and over. Short repeats like this are called microsatellites, and they are used for, among other things, DNA fingerprinting. A quantifier can apply to a whole group: (CA)+ means one or more copies of CA. Starting from the cleaned seq, use re.finditer with the pattern (CA){5,} to print every run of at least five CA repeats, with its start position and its length. Finally, try re.findall with the same pattern, and predict what it returns before you run it. Remember what re.findall does when the pattern contains a group (see Groups).

      121 tacacacaca caaaaatgaa gcacttactt tagaaagatt atggtaagca tgctggctca
'''

# Your code here

re.split is the regular-expression version of the string method .split. Where .split cuts the string at one fixed separator, re.split cuts it wherever the pattern matches. That helps when a colleague’s gene list was typed by hand:

%%sandbox
import re

genes = 'BRCA1, TP53;FOXP2   MYC,KRAS'
print(genes.split(','))
print(re.split(r'[,;\s]+', genes))

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Compiled patterns
When you call re.search, the re module first translates your pattern into an internal form it can run quickly. You can do that translation step yourself with re.compile, and you get a pattern object back. Like everything else in Python, it is an object with methods:

%%sandbox
import re

hinfi = re.compile('GA.TC')
print(type(hinfi))
print(hinfi.findall('TTGACTCAAGATTCCGAGTCA'))

re.findall('GA.TC', dna) says “Hey function, find this pattern in this string!”. hinfi.findall(dna) says “Hey pattern, find yourself in this string!”. It is the same function-versus-method story as capitalize. They do exactly the same thing. A compiled pattern is mostly a convenience: you give it a good name once and reuse it in many places. And print(type(...)) shows you that the match objects you have been using all along are objects of the class re.Match.

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
When not to use them
There is an old programmer joke: “If you have a problem and decide to solve it using regular expressions, you will have two problems”
Regular expressions are dense. A pattern that took you ten minutes to write can take you twenty to read a month later, and every character in it matters. So here is a rule of thumb. If you are looking for exact text, use in, .find, .count, .startswith or .split. They say what they do, and nobody needs to decode them. Reach for re when the thing you are looking for is a pattern: alternative letters at a position, repeats of unknown length, or pieces you want to pull out of a line.






Tip



Regular expressions could shortcut parts of the upcoming ORF project. Solve the project with the loops and slicing it asks for. The project is about decomposing a problem into functions, and a one-line pattern that you cannot debug teaches you nothing about that.

title: 60  Regular expressions
text:
Regular expressions and the assistant
Regular expressions are one of the things AI assistants are best at writing and one of the things people are worst at reading. That is an uncomfortable combination. A pattern looks the same whether it is right or wrong, so the only way to know is to test it on strings for which you decided the answer beforehand.

Exercise 60-18
AI: Explainer
Here is a pattern of the kind you will find in other people’s code for reading FASTA files:
r'^>(\S+)\s+(.*)$'
Give the assistant this pattern and nothing else, and ask it to translate it into English one piece at a time. Then, with the assistant closed, write down three header lines you predict it matches and two you predict it does not, and for the ones that match, what you expect in group 1 and group 2. Run them through re.search and compare. Your predictions settle it, not the explanation: if a result surprises you, find the piece of the translation that misled you or that you misread.

%%sandbox
import re

pattern = r'^>(\S+)\s+(.*)$'
for header in ['>NM_148900.4 Homo sapiens forkhead box P2',
               # your test headers here
              ]:
    match = re.search(pattern, header)
    if match:
        print(repr(header), '->', match.groups())
    else:
        print(repr(header), '-> no match')

Ask the assistant for two versions of the is_dna function from Anchors: one that uses re and one that uses no regular expression at all. Before you run either of them, decide what each one returns for '', the empty string, and whether the two versions agree. Then run both on 'ACGT', 'ACGN', 'acgt' and ''. title: 61  AI: Delegate the full problem
text:
This last level on the AI ladder, is not a badge you should pin on your vest just yet. This course has been short. Before you begin handing over the entire task to the AI, you need a lot more experience using the safe approach introduced in Chapter 51. That said, I know you will head off to fight Darth Vader before your jedi training is complete. So before you board your X-wing, here are some pointers that I hope you follow will.
The only way you can stay in control of your work with an AI, is to never ask it for something you do not know what is. Use the same steps that you have learned along the way, but delegate each one to the AI in separate steps.
Make sure you understand the problem you are going to solve. Begin by outlining to the AI, what the problem you want solved is. Say that you are not asking for code, but want to make sure you agree what the problem to solve is. Have it repeat back to you how it understood the problem you explained. Ask it for a Q and A, probing any unclear points and corner cases:


I need code that finds open reading frames (ORFs) in DNA sequence. Do not produce code until I way so. We need to first agree the problem at hand. Please quiz me on what the final product should look like.


When you are sure you agree on wha the problem is, make sure you agree on how to solve it. Say that you want it to it decompose the problem into functions explained by their docstrings and that these functions should be so small that each one can be tested reliably:


Please suggest how the required code can be decomposed into functions small enough to be tested reliably. Show me as function stubs with short docstrings.


Read and approve or ask it to revise the decomposition it suggests. When the decomposition is in place, ask it to write pytest tests for each function just like we did in Chapter 51:


Please write test functions in the same file to be run with pytest.


Read the tests to make sure the tests cover the relialistic use-cases you have in mind. Then ask it to fill in the bodies and run the tests you on the finished functions:


Now please fill in the function bodies and run the test suite on the finished functions.


Review the code to make sure you understand how it works. If you do not, ask the AI to explain it to you and/or write out the code more explicitly:


I don’t understand the code in the last function. Please add inline comments to explain each step of the code.

title: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?
text:
How this project is different
This chapter is a programming project where you assemble a bacterial plasmid from sequencing reads, find all its open reading frames, and then work out which of them are genes.
In Chapter 46 you searched the genome of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Sakai for open reading frames. The file you used held only the chromosome. The strain also carries a plasmid called pO157, a ring of DNA 92,721 bases long that is copied and passed on separately from the chromosome. Many of the genes that make this strain dangerous sit on that plasmid: the four hemolysin genes hlyA to hlyD that let the bacterium break open red blood cells, the protease EspP, and the large toxin gene toxB.
When you ran your ORF finder on the chromosome, you got many thousands of ORFs and translated all of them into “candidate proteins”. Most of them are not proteins at all. Any stretch of DNA has start codons, and an ATG followed by a hundred or so bases without a stop codon happens often enough by chance. Deciding which ORFs are genes is the problem of gene prediction, and every newly sequenced genome has to go through it before anyone can say what the organism can do. That is what you do in this project, for pO157.
The plasmid comes to you the way it would come off a sequencing machine. It was cut open at one place where there is no gene, so the ring became a line, and that line was read as overlapping pieces. So before you can look for genes, you have to put the plasmid back together. The project has four parts:
Begin by downloading the project. Open your instructing machines folder in VS Code. Then open a terminal (Terminal > New Terminal from the top menu) and run this command:
That puts the plasmidproject project folder straight into the projects folder inside your course folder, beside your notebooks.
If that fails, you can always click “Download project” in the top right corner of the page. This downloads a zip file to your Downloads folder that you need to then unpack and move into the projects folder of your student folder yourself.
The folder holds these files:
This is the week-twelve project, and as the course introduction says, at this point you get the goal and the data. Nobody tells you which functions to write. You decide how to break the problem into functions, what each one takes and returns, and how you test them. The assistant is open at AI: Developer, so you may hand it whole functions, under the rules of that badge.
There are only five functions whose names and formats are fixed, because the test file and the scorer have to be able to call them:
The test file checks each of them at one of four checkpoints, and it checks nothing else. It does not tell you which of your own functions is broken, only whether the checkpoint is reached. So write the tests for your own functions yourself, as you go.
Before you send the assistant a single prompt, open a file called criteria.md in the project folder. For each of the parts below, write the functions you plan, with what each takes and returns and two concrete examples, and write what would count as the part having failed. The assistant is useful once that plan exists. It can tell you about a case your examples miss, or write a function you have specified. If you ask it to “do the plasmid project”, you get back its plan instead of yours, and you have no criteria to judge it by. Keep notes for your logbook as you go: where the assistant was right, where it was wrong, and how you found out.

title: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?
text:
Checkpoint 1: Assemble the plasmid
plasmid_reads.txt holds 138 reads. Like the reads in Chapter 50, they have no sequencing errors, they all come from the same strand, and no read lies inside another. They are longer, though: each read is between 900 and 1,100 bases, and each read overlaps the next one along the plasmid by between 250 and 400 bases. The first read starts at the place where the plasmid was cut open.
Your assembly code from week ten nearly does the job. It will not do it unchanged, and the reason is the overlap rule. That code counted any overlap of more than two bases as a sign that two reads were neighbors. Before you run anything, think about how long a chance overlap between two unrelated 1,000-base reads can be, and how often one of 138 reads will have one. Then run your old code, see what happens, and change the rule.
Comparing every read to every other read is 138 × 137 = 18,906 overlap computations. With a sensible get_overlap that takes a few seconds. If your assembly takes minutes, look at that function first.
Write a function, assemble_plasmid, that takes one argument:

A string, which is the name of the file with the reads.

The function must return:

A string, which is the assembled plasmid, 92,721 bases long.
crumbs: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?

title: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?
text:
Checkpoint 2: Find the candidate ORFs
A candidate is an open reading frame: a start codon ATG followed, in the same reading frame, by the first stop codon (TAA, TAG or TGA). An ATG that never meets a stop codon before the sequence ends does not count. To compare your candidates with everyone else’s, and with the scorer, the rules for which candidates exist have to be exact:

Both strands. Genes can sit on either strand. The sequence of the other strand is the reverse complement of the plasmid, and you find its ORFs by searching that sequence the same way you search the plasmid. A candidate on the plasmid’s own strand has strand '+', one on the reverse complement has strand '-'.
Positions belong to the strand. start is the index of the first base of the start codon, and stop is the index of the first base of the stop codon, both counted in the sequence the ORF was found in. For a '-' candidate, that is the reverse complement.
One candidate per stop codon. Several start codons in the same frame can lead to the same stop codon, and your ORF finder from week nine returned one ORF for each of them. Here you keep only the longest, the one with the leftmost start codon. A gene has one stop codon, but where it starts is often uncertain.
No minimum length. An ATG followed directly by a stop codon is a candidate too. Deciding which candidates are too short to be genes is part of your job in the next two parts.

Each candidate is a dictionary with these four keys, and you may add more keys of your own if you find them useful:
{'strand': '+', 'start': 1203, 'stop': 2064, 'protein': 'MKLV...'}
protein is the translation from the start codon up to the stop codon, without the stop codon itself.
Write a function, find_candidates, that takes one argument:

A string, which is the plasmid sequence.

The function must return:

A list of candidate dictionaries, in any order.

Example usage:
find_candidates('ATGAAAATGCCCTAAGTCAAAACAT')
should return this list (in some order):
[{'strand': '+', 'start': 0, 'stop': 12, 'protein': 'MKMP'},
 {'strand': '-', 'start': 0, 'stop': 6, 'protein': 'MF'}]
The ATG at index 6 reaches the same stop codon as the one at index 0, so it gives no candidate of its own. The '-' candidate is found in the reverse complement, ATGTTTTGACTTAGGGCATTTTCAT. Check both by hand before you trust your code with them. On the assembled plasmid you should find 1,922 candidates.
crumbs: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?

title: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?
text:
Checkpoint 3: Sensitivity and specificity
To know whether a prediction is any good, you need something to compare it with. The public record of pO157 in GenBank annotates 85 genes on it, and the module genescore.py knows which of your candidates they are. It keeps them as scrambled codes, so you cannot read them off, but it can count. Give it your predictions, which are some of your candidates, and all the candidates:
from genescore import score

counts = score(predictions, candidates)
and it returns a dictionary with four counts:
{'TP': 61, 'FP': 21, 'TN': 1816, 'FN': 24}




annotated gene
not annotated




predicted gene
TP (true positive)
FP (false positive)


not predicted
FN (false negative)
TN (true negative)



A candidate is matched to an annotated gene by its strand and its stop codon, for the same reason as above: the stop codon is certain, the start is not.
Two numbers summarize the table. The sensitivity is the fraction of the true genes that you found, and the specificity is the fraction of the non-genes that you correctly left out:
\[
\text{sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \qquad\qquad \text{specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}
\]
Write two functions, sensitivity and specificity, that each take one argument:

A dictionary of counts as returned by score.

Each function must return:

A float between 0 and 1.

Before you use them, decide what sensitivity and specificity you get if you predict that every candidate is a gene, and what you get if you predict that none of them are. Then check with score.
The simplest evidence you have is length, since a long ORF is unlikely to happen by chance. Use it as your baseline: predict that every candidate whose protein is at least some minimum length is a gene, and compute sensitivity and specificity for minimum lengths 0, 25, 50, and so on up to 300. Put the results in a table and in a plot (Chapter 48). As the minimum length goes up, one of the two numbers rises and the other falls. Every other piece of evidence in this project is judged against this curve: at the same specificity, does it find more genes than length alone?
score writes a line to score_log.txt every time you call it. Keep that file. It comes up again in Checkpoint 4.
crumbs: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?

title: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?
text:
Checkpoint 4: Weigh the evidence
Now comes the main part of the project. A gene leaves more traces in the DNA than its length, and your job is to find some of them, measure what each is worth, and combine them in a function predict_genes(candidates, plasmid) that returns the candidates you predict are genes. The checkpoint test only checks that it returns some of the candidates. How good the prediction is, you measure yourself with score.
Write each piece of evidence as its own function that looks at one candidate (and the plasmid, if it needs it) and returns True or False, or a number. Then you can measure each piece on its own before you combine them. Here are some ideas. You are expected to try at least two of them, or ideas of your own, in addition to length.
A ribosome binding site. In bacteria, the ribosome finds the start of a gene by pairing with a short sequence a few bases upstream of the start codon, the Shine-Dalgarno sequence, which is close to AGGAGG. Real genes often have part of it about 5 to 15 bases before their ATG, and chance ORFs rarely do. Remember that for a '-' candidate, “upstream” is in the reverse complement.
Similarity to known proteins. A gene on pO157 often has a relative on another plasmid. proteins.fasta holds 367 proteins from four plasmids related to pO157: the F plasmid of E. coli K-12, the virulence plasmid of Shigella flexneri, a plasmid of Salmonella Typhimurium, and a plasmid from another disease-causing E. coli. Proteins nearly identical to pO157’s own were removed, so a match only ever points to a relative. You can score a candidate protein against each of them with a local alignment, as in the Biopython chapter:
from Bio import Align
from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices

aligner = Align.PairwiseAligner()
aligner.mode = "local"
aligner.substitution_matrix = substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62")
aligner.open_gap_score = -10
aligner.extend_gap_score = -0.5

print(aligner.score("MKLVINGKTLKGEITVE", "MKLVLNGKSLRGEVTVE"))
score is much faster than align when you need only the number. Even so, searching all candidates of 30 amino acids or more against all 367 proteins takes about a minute, so compute the scores once and save them to a file. Then decide how high a score has to be to mean anything. You can find out without looking at the answers: shuffle the letters of some candidate proteins, search with those, and see how high a score you get from chance alone.
Codon usage. In Chapter 42 you saw that a genome does not use all codons for an amino acid equally. Real genes share that preference, and chance ORFs do not. The longest candidates, say 300 amino acids or more, are almost all genes, so you can compute a reference codon usage from them and ask how well each shorter candidate fits it.
Overlap. Genes on a plasmid are packed tightly but rarely overlap much. A candidate lying almost entirely inside a much longer candidate, on the other strand or in another frame, is probably a shadow of the longer gene rather than a gene of its own.
A shuffled plasmid. This one is not evidence about a candidate. It is a way to check your predictor without the scorer. Shuffle the bases of the plasmid with random.shuffle, find the candidates in the shuffled sequence, and run predict_genes on them. The shuffled sequence has no genes, so every prediction there is a false positive. If your predictor finds many genes in it, it will find just as many false ones in the real plasmid.
Your own idea. If you know something about genes that none of these use, try it. That counts as much as any idea on the list.
When you combine the pieces, keep in mind what the scorer is. Every time you call score, you learn a little about the answers, and if you adjust your thresholds until the score is as high as it can get, you end up with a predictor tuned to this one plasmid that does worse on the next. Set your thresholds from biology and from shuffled sequences where you can, and use score to measure the result. score_log.txt will show how many times you looked.
crumbs: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?

title: 62  Project: Which ORFs are genes?
text:
Are the annotations right?
When your predictor is done, look at the false positives it is most confident about, for example the ones with the highest homology scores. Use the GenBank record of the plasmid (RefSeq NC_002128.1, read as in the Biopython chapter) to see what is annotated near them. Before you call them mistakes, consider where the answers came from. The record says its gene annotation was made by a gene-prediction program and compared with what the original scientists submitted. Of the 85 annotated genes, 37 are called “hypothetical protein”, which means nobody has shown that they make a protein. A false positive with a strong match to a known protein might be a mistake in your predictor, or it might be a mistake in the annotation. Write down which you think it is, and why.
